terms.section: 1.1 Introduction to Operations and Supply Chain Management
terms.short: The part of a business organization responsible for producing goods and/or services.
terms.more: Operations is a line function, the core of every business, profit or nonprofit; if a business were a car, operations would be the engine.

confusedWith.note: the management of the systems or processes that create goods and/or provide services

terms.trap: "The operations function consists of all activities indirectly related to producing goods or providing services" is FALSE: it is the part responsible for producing them.

terms.section: 1.1 Introduction to Operations and Supply Chain Management
terms.short: The management of systems or processes that create goods and/or provide services.

confusedWith.note: the function itself: the part of the organization that produces goods and/or services

terms.section: 1.1 Introduction to Operations and Supply Chain Management
terms.short: Finance, marketing, and operations: the three basic functions that all business organizations have.
terms.more: Finance secures and allocates financial resources; marketing assesses consumer wants and needs and sells and promotes; operations produces the goods or provides the services.

confusedWith.note: the two line functions are operations and sales

terms.trap: "Business organizations have four basic functions" is FALSE: there are three (finance, marketing, operations), and IT, engineering, HR, accounting and supply chain are not among them.

terms.short: Operations and sales, the two primary functions of a business; all other functions, such as accounting, finance, marketing and IT, support them.

confusedWith.note: finance, marketing, and operations

terms.trap: "Finance is a line function" or "marketing and operations are the two line functions" is FALSE: the two line functions are operations and sales.

terms.section: 1.1 Introduction to Operations and Supply Chain Management
terms.short: Physical items, including raw materials, parts, subassemblies such as motherboards, and final products such as cell phones and automobiles.
terms.more: Producing goods results in a tangible output. Goods can be stored as inventory and are usually easier to patent than services.

confusedWith.note: an act; intangible, cannot be stored, provided on demand

terms.section: 1.1 Introduction to Operations and Supply Chain Management
terms.short: Activities that provide some combination of time, location, form, or psychological value.
terms.more: Delivering a service generally implies an act, such as a physician's exam or lawn care. Services are intangible and cannot be stored, so they must be provided on demand.

confusedWith.note: tangible physical items that can be stored

terms.trap: "Services can be inventoried" is FALSE: services cannot be stored and must be provided on demand.

terms.section: 1.1 Introduction to Operations and Supply Chain Management
terms.short: The sequence of organizations, with their facilities, functions and activities, involved in producing and delivering a product or service.
terms.more: It begins with basic suppliers of raw materials and extends all the way to the final customer. Supply chains are both external and internal to the organization, and each link is a customer of the previous link and a supplier to the next.

confusedWith.note: the management of that sequence

terms.trap: "Supply chains are only external to the organization" is FALSE: they are both external and internal.

terms.section: 1.1 Introduction to Operations and Supply Chain Management
terms.short: Management of the sequence of internal and external facilities, functions, and activities involved in producing and delivering a product or service.
terms.more: Operations and supply chains are intrinsically linked: no business organization can exist without both.

confusedWith.note: the sequence of organizations itself

terms.trap: "Not every organization needs both operations and a supply chain" is FALSE: no business organization can exist without both.

terms.section: 1.1 Introduction to Operations and Supply Chain Management
terms.short: The difference between the cost of inputs and the value or price of outputs.
terms.more: Adding value during the transformation process is the essence of the operations function. For nonprofits, the value of outputs is their value to society.
terms.trap: "Value-added equals input cost minus output price" is FALSE: it is the value or price of outputs minus the cost of inputs.

terms.section: 1.1 Introduction to Operations and Supply Chain Management
terms.short: A combination of goods and services sold together.
terms.more: Most companies sell product packages because there are relatively few pure goods or pure services. They make operations more interesting but more challenging to manage.

terms.section: 1.1 Introduction to Operations and Supply Chain Management
terms.short: Measurements taken at various points in the transformation process.

confusedWith.note: comparing those measurements to standards to decide whether corrective action is needed

terms.trap: "Feedback is comparing measurements with standards to decide whether corrective action is needed" is FALSE: that is control; feedback is the measurements themselves.

terms.section: 1.1 Introduction to Operations and Supply Chain Management
terms.short: Comparing feedback measurements with previously established standards to decide whether corrective action is needed.

confusedWith.note: the measurements themselves

terms.trap: "Control is the measurements taken at various points in the transformation process" is FALSE: that is feedback; control compares those measurements with standards.

terms.section: 1.2 Production of Goods versus Providing Services
terms.short: In high-contact services, each interaction between server and customer, which the customer judges every time the service occurs.
The time between submitting an order and receiving it.
terms.more: The greater the potential variability of demand and lead time, the greater the need for additional stock to reduce shortage risk.

terms.short: One or more actions that transform inputs into outputs.
terms.more: The central role of all management is process management. A major process can consist of many subprocesses, each with its own goals.

terms.short: Managing business processes through three activities: process design, process execution, and process monitoring.
terms.more: Its two basic aspects for operations and supply chain management are managing processes to meet demand and dealing with process variability.

terms.short: Variation in demand from trends and seasonal patterns; generally predictable and particularly important for capacity planning.
terms.more: One of the four basic sources of variation: variety of goods or services offered, structural variation in demand, random variation, and assignable variation.

confusedWith.note: natural variability that is unpredictable and always present

terms.trap: "Structural variation is generally unpredictable" is FALSE: it is generally predictable.

terms.short: Natural, inherent variation from the combined influence of countless minor factors, each so unimportant that eliminating it would have negligible impact.
terms.more: Also called chance variation; Deming called it common variability. Every process has it. Older machines generally show more natural variability than newer ones.

confusedWith.note: nonrandom, special variation whose sources can be identified and eliminated

terms.trap: "Random variation is special variation" is FALSE: Deming called random variation common; assignable variation is special.

terms.short: Nonrandom variation whose main sources can usually be identified (assigned to a specific cause) and eliminated.
terms.more: Deming called it special variation. Typical sources: tool wear, equipment needing adjustment, defective materials, human factors (carelessness, fatigue, distractions, failure to follow procedures), and problems with measuring devices.

confusedWith.note: natural, common variation that cannot be corrected

terms.trap: "Assignable variation is common variation" is FALSE: Deming called assignable variation special; random variation is common.

terms.short: Decisions on capacity, facility location, layout, product and service planning, and equipment acquisition; usually long-term, strategic commitments.
terms.more: System design essentially determines many parameters of system operation, such as costs, space, capacities and quality.

confusedWith.note: personnel, inventory, scheduling, project management, quality assurance; tactical and operational

terms.trap: "System design decisions always require long-term commitments" is FALSE: they usually, but not always, do.

terms.short: Decisions on management of personnel, inventory planning and control, scheduling, project management, and quality assurance; generally tactical and operational.
terms.more: In many instances the operations manager is more involved in these day-to-day operating decisions than in system design decisions.

confusedWith.note: capacity, location, layout, product and service planning, equipment; strategic

terms.trap: "Scheduling and quality assurance are system design decisions" is FALSE: they are system operation decisions.

terms.short: An abstraction of reality; a simplified representation of something.
terms.more: Three classifications, from least to most abstract: physical, schematic, mathematical. Models are decision-making aids that omit unimportant details; their limitations include that their use does not guarantee good decisions.
terms.trap: "Models guarantee good decisions" is FALSE: the use of models does not guarantee good decisions.

terms.short: Models that look like their real-life counterparts, such as miniature cars or scale-model buildings; the least abstract kind.
terms.more: Their advantage is visual correspondence with reality.

confusedWith.note: more abstract: graphs, charts, blueprints
most abstract: numbers, formulas, symbols

terms.trap: "Physical models are the most abstract" is FALSE: mathematical models are the most abstract.

terms.short: Models more abstract than physical ones, such as graphs, charts, blueprints and drawings, that are relatively simple to construct and change.
terms.more: They keep some degree of visual correspondence with reality.

confusedWith.note: look like their real-life counterparts
most abstract: numbers, formulas, symbols

terms.trap: "Blueprints are physical models" is FALSE: blueprints are schematic models.

terms.short: The most abstract models, using numbers, formulas and symbols; they don't look like their counterparts but are usually easiest to manipulate.

confusedWith.note: look like their real-life counterparts
graphs, charts, blueprints; some visual correspondence

terms.trap: "Mathematical models are the hardest to manipulate" is FALSE: they are usually the easiest to manipulate.

terms.short: Collecting, analyzing, and presenting data using statistics, math, and computers for decision making.
terms.more: Four types: descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive.

terms.short: Summarizing data, for example with averages, graphs, frequency distributions, and pie charts.

confusedWith.note: why something happened
what will happen
how to influence a desired change

terms.short: Determining why something happened, such as what caused a process to produce unacceptable output.
terms.more: Tool: quality control charts.

confusedWith.note: summarizing data
what will happen
how to influence a desired change

terms.trap: "Control charts are a descriptive analytics tool" is FALSE: they are a diagnostic tool.

terms.short: Focusing on what will happen, such as future demand and its effect on operations.
terms.more: Tool: forecasting.

confusedWith.note: summarizing data
why something happened
how to influence a desired change

terms.trap: "Forecasting is prescriptive analytics" is FALSE: forecasting is predictive.

terms.short: Analyzing data to determine how to influence a desired change.
terms.more: Strategy formulation often relies on it; example: reconfiguring a system to reduce waiting times.

confusedWith.note: summarizing data
why something happened
what will happen

terms.short: A set of interrelated parts that must work together.
terms.more: A systems perspective holds that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts, so the objectives of the organization as a whole take precedence over those of any one subsystem.
terms.trap: "Subsystem objectives take precedence over those of the organization as a whole" is FALSE: the organization as a whole takes precedence.

terms.short: Typically a relatively few issues or items are very important, so dealing with them has a disproportionately large impact on results.
terms.more: One of the most important and pervasive concepts in operations management; it applies at all levels of management and to every aspect of decision making, professional and personal.
terms.trap: "The Pareto phenomenon applies only to quality or inventory, or only at top management" is FALSE: it applies at all levels and to every aspect of decision making.

terms.section: 1.8 The Historical Evolution of Operations Management
terms.short: Highly skilled workers using simple, flexible tools to produce goods according to customer specifications.
terms.more: Four shortcomings: slow and costly; replacement parts also custom made; no economies of scale (costs did not fall as volume rose); many small companies each with its own standards.

confusedWith.note: low or semiskilled workers, specialized equipment, standardized goods
skilled workers and flexible equipment, with the high volume of mass production

terms.trap: "Craft production had economies of scale" is FALSE: production costs did not decrease as volume increased.

terms.section: 1.8 The Historical Evolution of Operations Management
terms.short: Large volumes of standardized goods produced by low or semiskilled workers using highly specialized, often costly, equipment.
terms.more: Henry Ford introduced it to the automotive industry; interchangeable parts were perhaps the key concept that launched it.

confusedWith.note: highly skilled workers, simple flexible tools, customer specifications
skilled workers, flexible equipment, less space, inventory and workers

terms.trap: "Mass production uses highly skilled workers with flexible tools" is FALSE: that describes craft production.

terms.section: 1.8 The Historical Evolution of Operations Management
terms.short: Standardized parts made so that any part in a batch fits any unit on the line, removing the need for custom fitting.
terms.more: Sometimes attributed to Eli Whitney (muskets, 1790 in Table 1.5); perhaps the key concept that launched mass production. Ford achieved it by standardizing gauges.

confusedWith.note: Adam Smith; splitting an operation into many small tasks

terms.section: 1.8 The Historical Evolution of Operations Management
terms.short: Dividing an operation into a series of many small tasks and assigning each worker to one task.
terms.more: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations (1776). The tasks are so narrow that virtually no skill is required.

confusedWith.note: Eli Whitney; standardized parts that fit any unit

terms.section: 1.8 The Historical Evolution of Operations Management
terms.short: Frederick Winslow Taylor's approach to management based on observation, measurement, analysis and improvement of work methods, and economic incentives.
terms.more: Taylor, the father of scientific management, sought the best method for each job. Publicity from the 1911 congressional hearings actually helped it achieve wide acceptance.
terms.trap: "The congressional hearings led to the rejection of scientific management" is FALSE: the publicity helped it achieve wide acceptance.

terms.section: 1.8 The Historical Evolution of Operations Management
terms.short: Douglas McGregor's view that workers do not like to work and must be controlled, rewarded and punished; results in an adversarial environment.

confusedWith.note: workers enjoy work and become committed
Ouchi's blend of Japanese and Western approaches

terms.trap: "Theory X holds that workers enjoy work and become committed" is FALSE: that is Theory Y; Theory X holds that workers dislike work and must be controlled.

terms.section: 1.8 The Historical Evolution of Operations Management
terms.short: Douglas McGregor's view that workers enjoy the physical and mental aspects of work and become committed; results in empowered, more cooperative workers.

confusedWith.note: workers dislike work and must be controlled
Ouchi's blend of Japanese and Western approaches

terms.trap: "Theory Y holds that workers do not like to work and must be controlled" is FALSE: that is Theory X; Theory Y workers enjoy work and become committed.

terms.section: 1.8 The Historical Evolution of Operations Management
terms.short: William Ouchi's combination of the Japanese approach with the traditional Western approach to managing workers.
terms.more: Japanese: lifetime employment, employee problem solving, consensus building. Western: short-term employment, specialists, individual decision making and responsibility.

confusedWith.note: McGregor; workers dislike work
McGregor; workers enjoy work

terms.trap: "Theory Z is McGregor's" or "Theory Z is purely Japanese" is FALSE: it is Ouchi's blend of Japanese and Western approaches.

terms.short: The use of the internet to transact business, with both customers and suppliers.
terms.more: Business-to-business transactions such as e-procurement represent an increasing share of e-business.

confusedWith.note: consumer-business transactions only

terms.trap: "E-business covers only consumer transactions" is FALSE: that is e-commerce; e-business includes business-to-business.

terms.short: Consumer-business transactions over the internet, such as buying online or requesting information.
terms.more: It is the part of e-business most familiar to the public.

confusedWith.note: all use of the internet to transact business, including B2B

terms.trap: "E-commerce means business-to-business transactions" is FALSE: e-commerce is consumer-business; e-procurement is B2B.

terms.short: Applications of scientific knowledge to the development and improvement of goods and services and/or the processes that produce or provide them.
terms.more: Three aspects matter in process selection and layout: product technology, processing technology, and information technology.

terms.short: The methods, procedures, and equipment used to produce goods and provide services, both within the organization and in the supply chain.

confusedWith.note: discovery and development of new products and services
computers and electronics to store, process and send information, such as bar codes

terms.trap: "Methods, procedures, and equipment describe product technology" is FALSE: they describe process technology.

terms.short: A method to maximize revenue from fixed operating capacity by influencing demand through price manipulation; also called yield management.
terms.more: Used by airlines, cruise lines, hotels, amusement parks and rental car companies, and also trucking and public utilities.

confusedWith.note: responding quickly through a flexible system
using less space, inventory and workers

terms.trap: "Revenue management maximizes revenue by increasing capacity" is FALSE: it works on fixed capacity by influencing demand through price.

terms.short: Statistically, no more than 3.4 defects per million opportunities; conceptually, a program to reduce defects for lower costs and better customer satisfaction.
terms.more: Motorola pioneered it in the 1980s and trademarked the term. It applies tools to selected projects aligned with strategy and has a management component and a technical component.
terms.trap: "Selecting projects and training people belong to the technical component" is FALSE: they are management; reducing variation, statistical methods and DMAIC are technical.

terms.short: The ability of an organization to respond quickly to demands or opportunities, by keeping a flexible system that adapts to changes in volume or offerings.
terms.more: Important with increasingly shorter product life cycles. Example: Zara and H&M, near low-cost producers in Romania and Turkey, get trendy fashion to shelves quickly.

confusedWith.note: using less space, inventory and workers
price manipulation to maximize revenue from fixed capacity

terms.short: Systems that use much less space, inventory, and workers than mass production for comparable output, with a highly skilled workforce and flexible equipment.
terms.more: Lean production emerged in the 1990s and combines the high volume and low unit cost of mass production with the variety and flexibility of craft production. Workers are generalists in teams, and team success matters more than individual creativity.

confusedWith.note: low or semiskilled workers, specialized equipment
skilled workers, simple flexible tools, low volume
responding quickly through a flexible system

terms.trap: "Lean uses low-skilled workers and specialized equipment" is FALSE: that is mass production; lean uses a highly skilled workforce and flexible equipment.

terms.section: 1.10 Key Issues for Today's Business Operations
terms.short: Buying goods or services instead of producing or providing them in-house.
terms.more: Increasing outsourcing is one reason managing supply chains is essential; companies must monitor the safety of outsourced goods. Outsourcing goods production also increases transportation costs, fuel use and carbon released.

terms.section: 1.10 Key Issues for Today's Business Operations
terms.short: Service and production processes that use resources in ways that do not harm ecological systems supporting both current and future human existence.

confusedWith.note: the CO2 generated by operations and supply chains
touting only minor environmental improvements

terms.trap: "Sustainability measures are limited to environmental and economic measures" is FALSE: they often include social criteria too.

terms.section: 1.10 Key Issues for Today's Business Operations
terms.short: The amount of carbon dioxide generated by an organization's operations and its supply chains.

confusedWith.note: using resources without harming ecological systems, now or in future
touting only minor environmental improvements

terms.section: 1.10 Key Issues for Today's Business Operations
terms.short: Touting only minor environmental improvements to appear environmentally friendly.
terms.more: It can even mean citing regulation-mandated changes the company lobbied against, such as automakers touting electric vehicles.

confusedWith.note: using resources without harming ecological systems
the CO2 generated by operations and supply chains

terms.section: 1.10 Key Issues for Today's Business Operations
terms.short: Standards of behavior that guide how one should act in various situations.
terms.more: The Markkula Center's five principles for thinking ethically are the Utilitarian, Rights, Fairness, Common Good, and Virtue principles.

confusedWith.note: a sequence of steps to guide decisions
an organization's own document

terms.section: 1.10 Key Issues for Today's Business Operations
terms.short: A sequence of steps intended to guide thinking and subsequent decisions or actions.
terms.more: The Markkula framework has 5 steps: recognize an ethical issue; know the pertinent facts; evaluate options by ethical principle; identify the best option and ask how someone you respect would view it; in retrospect, consider the effect and what you can learn.

confusedWith.note: standards of behavior
an organization's own document

terms.section: 1.10 Key Issues for Today's Business Operations
terms.short: Systems increasingly used for real-time information sharing among organizations and their major supply chain partners.
How effective an organization is in the marketplace relative to other organizations offering similar products or services.
terms.more: Organizations compete through some combination of price, delivery time, and product or service differentiation (3). Operations and marketing have a major impact on it, and productivity has a direct impact on it.

terms.short: The chapter's seven chief reasons organizations fail, starting with neglecting operations strategy.
terms.more: The 7: neglecting operations strategy; failing to use strengths and opportunities or recognize competitive threats; too much emphasis on short-term financial performance at the expense of R&D; too much emphasis on product and service design and not enough on process design and improvement; neglecting investments in capital and human resources; poor internal communications and cooperation; failing to consider customer wants and needs.
terms.trap: "Too much emphasis on R&D at the expense of short-term financial performance" is FALSE: the reason is too much emphasis on short-term financial performance at the expense of R&D.

terms.short: The ability to respond to changes in design features, volume demanded, or mix of products or services.
terms.more: High flexibility is a competitive advantage in a changeable environment.

confusedWith.note: a strategic approach that uses flexibility, blended with cost, quality and reliability, to prosper amid change

terms.short: The reason for an organization's existence.
terms.more: It is expressed in a mission statement, which is the basis for organizational goals. Planning hierarchy: mission, goals, organizational strategies, functional strategies, tactics, operations.

confusedWith.note: goals give the detail and scope of the mission
strategies are plans (roadmaps) for achieving goals

terms.short: The statement of an organization's mission; for a business it should answer "What business are we in?"
terms.more: Examples: Microsoft (help people and businesses realize their full potential), Verizon (help people and businesses communicate), Starbucks (inspire and nurture the human spirit, one cup and one neighborhood at a time).

terms.short: Statements that give more detail and describe the scope of the mission, serving as the foundation for organizational strategies.
terms.more: The mission statement is the basis for goals; goals must be aligned with the mission.

confusedWith.note: the reason for the organization's existence
if goals are destinations, strategies are the roadmaps

terms.trap: "Strategies are the basis for goals" is FALSE: goals serve as the foundation for developing strategies.

terms.short: Plans for achieving goals: if goals are destinations, strategies are the roadmaps.
terms.more: Strategies provide focus for decision making and can be the main reason for an organization's success or failure.

confusedWith.note: the destinations that strategies aim at
the more specific methods and actions used to carry out strategies

terms.short: Overall strategies relating to the entire organization, giving it overall direction; broad in scope.
terms.more: They guide the organization by providing direction for, and alignment of, the goals and strategies of the functional units.

confusedWith.note: strategies for one functional area
narrower in scope, dealing primarily with operations

terms.short: Strategies for each functional area, such as finance, marketing and operations, that should support the organizational strategies.
terms.more: They are narrower in scope and should take each other into account: complementary functional strategies are an opportunity, conflicting ones are a threat.

confusedWith.note: broad strategies for the entire organization

terms.short: The methods and actions used to accomplish strategies; more specific than strategies, they are the "how to."
terms.more: Operations are the actual "doing" below tactics. Example (Rita): strategy = get a college education; tactics = choose a college and major and decide how to finance it.

confusedWith.note: the broader plans that tactics carry out

terms.trap: "Tactics are more general than strategies" is FALSE: tactics are more specific than strategies.

terms.short: The three primary business strategies: low cost, responsiveness, and differentiation from competitors.
terms.more: Responsiveness is the ability to respond to changing demands; differentiation can come from features, quality, reputation, or customer service. Some firms combine them (Amazon: low cost, quick reliable delivery, excellent customer service).

terms.short: Special attributes or abilities possessed by an organization that give it a competitive edge.
terms.more: Also called distinctive competence. The most effective organizations base them on customer needs and what the competition is doing; strategies and core competencies need to be aligned.

confusedWith.note: monitoring external events and trends

terms.short: The monitoring of events and trends that present either threats or opportunities for the organization.
terms.more: Typically covers competitors' activities; changing consumer needs; legal, economic, political, and environmental issues; and the potential for new markets.

confusedWith.note: the organization's own special abilities that give it an edge

terms.short: Analysis of strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats; often regarded as the link between organizational strategy and operations strategy.
terms.more: Strengths and weaknesses have an internal focus and are typically evaluated by operations people; opportunities and threats have an external focus and are typically evaluated by marketing people.

confusedWith.note: Porter's alternative to SWOT

terms.trap: "Strengths and weaknesses are external and evaluated by marketing" is FALSE: they are internal and typically evaluated by operations people.

terms.short: Michael Porter's model of five forces, used as an alternative to SWOT analysis.
terms.more: The 5: threat of new competition; threat of substitute products or services; bargaining power of customers; bargaining power of suppliers; intensity of competition.

confusedWith.note: strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats

terms.trap: "Bargaining power of employees is one of the five forces" is FALSE: it is not on the list (nor is government power or threat of regulation).

terms.short: Characteristics customers see as minimum standards of acceptability for a product to be considered for purchase.
terms.more: Necessary but may not be sufficient. Price, delivery reliability, delivery speed, and quality can each be either an order qualifier or an order winner, depending on the situation.

confusedWith.note: characteristics perceived as better than the competition

terms.trap: "Over time, an order qualifier may become an order winner" is FALSE: the direction is the reverse; an order winner may become an order qualifier.

terms.short: Characteristics of an organization's goods or services that cause them to be perceived as better than the competition.
terms.more: Over time an order winner may become an order qualifier. Marketing must determine order winners and qualifiers and their relative importance, and communicate it to operations.

confusedWith.note: minimum standards needed just to be considered

terms.trap: "Operations determines the order winners" is FALSE: marketing makes that determination and communicates it to operations.

terms.short: Developing strategy by weighing how organizations compete and the organization's own strengths and weaknesses, to take advantage of its core competencies.
terms.more: Four key steps: link strategy directly to the mission or vision statement; assess strengths, weaknesses, threats and opportunities and identify core competencies; identify order winners and order qualifiers; focus on one or two strategies.
terms.trap: "Focus on as many strategies as possible" is FALSE: the step is to focus on one or two strategies.

terms.short: Eight outside factors to assess when formulating strategy, from economic and political conditions to customers, suppliers and markets.
terms.more: The 8: economic conditions, political conditions, legal environment, technology, competition, customers, suppliers, markets. Technology appears on both the external and internal lists.

confusedWith.note: the organization's own resources: human resources, facilities, finances, products, technology, other

terms.trap: "Cost of capital is an external economic condition" is FALSE: cost of capital is an internal financial resource; interest rates are external.

terms.short: Six factors within the organization to assess when formulating strategy, such as human resources, facilities and financial resources.
terms.more: The 6: human resources; facilities and equipment; financial resources; products and services; technology; other factors (patents, labor relations, company or product image, distribution channels, and more).

confusedWith.note: economic, political, legal, technology, competition, customers, suppliers, markets

terms.trap: "Patents and labor relations are external factors" is FALSE: they are internal "other factors" (patent laws fall under the external legal environment).

terms.short: A database of profiles of over 3,000 businesses used to guide strategic thinking, generate benchmarks, and test strategies.
terms.more: Run by the Strategic Planning Institute; businesses are primarily in the U.S., Canada and western Europe. It helps show which strategies work best in which business environments.

terms.short: A strategy that specifies how the supply chain should function to achieve supply chain goals.
terms.more: It should be aligned with the business strategy, and establishes how to work with suppliers and policies on customer relationships and sustainability.

terms.short: Three areas of goals: economic (financial well-being), environmental (natural ecological well-being), and social (wellness of human conditions).
terms.more: Employee wages, profits and shareholder wealth are economic; quality of work life and community impacts are social. Companies can weight the three, with the values summing to 100%.
terms.trap: "Employee wages are a social sustainability goal" is FALSE: they are an economic goal.

terms.short: Strategy narrower in scope than organization strategy, dealing primarily with the operations aspect of the organization.
terms.more: It relates to products, processes, methods, operating resources, quality, costs, lead times, and scheduling. It should not be formulated independently of organization strategy and must be consistent with it.

confusedWith.note: broad strategy covering the entire organization

terms.trap: "Operations strategy was emphasized over marketing and finance in the 1970s" is FALSE: in the 1970s and early 1980s it was often neglected in favor of marketing and financial strategies.

terms.short: Eleven decision areas of operations strategy, most of which have cost implications.
terms.more: The 11: product and service design, capacity, process selection and layout, work design, location, quality, inventory, maintenance, scheduling, supply chains, projects. Quality and time have universal strategic importance.

terms.short: Strategies that focus on maintaining or improving the quality of an organization's products or services.
terms.more: Quality helps both attract and retain customers. Such a strategy can be part of another strategy, such as cost reduction, increased productivity, or time.

confusedWith.note: focus on reducing the time to accomplish activities

terms.short: Strategies that focus on reducing the time required to accomplish various activities, to improve customer service and beat slower rivals.
terms.more: By reducing time, costs are generally less, productivity is higher, quality tends to be higher, innovations appear sooner, and customer service improves. Six areas: planning, product/service design, processing, changeover, delivery, and response time for complaints.

confusedWith.note: focus on maintaining or improving quality

terms.trap: "Reducing time generally increases costs" is FALSE: by reducing time, costs are generally less.

terms.short: The time needed to change from producing one product or service to another.
terms.more: Involves new equipment settings or attachments, methods, equipment, schedules, or materials. One of six areas of time reduction.
terms.trap: "Changing equipment settings to switch products is processing time" is FALSE: that is changeover time.

terms.short: A strategic approach that uses flexibility to adapt and prosper in an environment of change.
terms.more: Agility blends several competencies (cost, quality, reliability) along with flexibility, and requires a planned system of people, flexible equipment, and information technology.

confusedWith.note: the ability to respond to changes in design, volume, or mix

terms.section: 2.6 Transforming Strategy into Action: The Balanced Scorecard
terms.short: A top-down management system organizations use to clarify their vision and strategy and transform them into action.
terms.more: Introduced in the early 1990s by Robert Kaplan and David Norton, with four perspectives: financial, customer, internal business processes, and learning and growth. Limitations: no role in strategy formulation, little attention to suppliers and government regulation, and missing community, environmental and sustainability issues.
terms.trap: "The balanced scorecard is used to formulate strategy" is FALSE: it has no role in strategy formulation; it helps with implementation.

terms.short: An index that measures output (goods and services) relative to the input (labor, materials, energy, other resources) used to produce it: output divided by input.
terms.more: Operations management is chiefly responsible for it. It is particularly important for a low-cost strategy, and for a nation it is a key factor in the rate of inflation and the standard of living.

confusedWith.note: narrower: getting the most out of a fixed set of resources
the change in productivity relative to the previous period
good output relative to raw material input

terms.trap: "Productivity is the ratio of input to output" is FALSE: it is output divided by input.

terms.short: The increase in productivity from one period to the next, relative to productivity in the preceding period.
terms.more: Computed as (current - previous) / previous x 100; for a nation, its rate is of great importance.

confusedWith.note: the output-to-input ratio itself

terms.trap: "Productivity growth divides the change by current productivity" is FALSE: it divides by the previous period's productivity.

terms.short: A productivity measure based on a single input, such as output per labor hour or per machine hour.
terms.more: Partial measures are often of greatest use in operations management. Types: labor, machine, capital, and energy productivity.

confusedWith.note: more than one input
all inputs

terms.trap: "Total measures are most useful in operations management" is FALSE: partial measures are often of greatest use in OM.

terms.short: A productivity measure based on more than one input, such as output divided by labor plus machine.
terms.more: The inputs must be in a common unit of measurement (for example, cost) for all factors in the denominator.

confusedWith.note: a single input
all inputs

terms.short: A productivity measure based on all inputs: goods or services produced divided by all inputs used to produce them.
terms.more: The choice among partial, multifactor and total measures depends primarily on the purpose of the measurement.

confusedWith.note: a single input
more than one input

terms.short: The ratio of output of good product to total output.
terms.more: Inspection at key points guides improvement to reduce scrap and improve yield.

terms.short: Five categories of factors that affect productivity: methods, capital, quality, technology, and management.
terms.more: Examples: standardizing procedures (methods); incentive plans (capital, as listed in this edition); scrap rates (quality); computer viruses (technology); turnover, layoffs, safety and training (management). Technology alone does not guarantee productivity gains.
terms.trap: "Workers are the main determinant of productivity" is FALSE: that is a common misconception; many past gains came from other sources such as technological improvements.

terms.short: Six steps to improve productivity, starting with developing productivity measures for all operations.
terms.more: The 6: develop measures for all operations; look at the system as a whole when deciding which operations are most critical (bottlenecks); develop methods for improvement; set reasonable goals; make clear management supports improvement; measure improvements and publicize them. Plus: don't confuse productivity with efficiency.

terms.short: A narrower concept than productivity: getting the most out of a fixed set of resources.
terms.more: Lawn mower example: efficiency is the best way to use the hand mower; productivity also considers using a power mower.

confusedWith.note: broader: effective use of overall resources

terms.trap: "Improving efficiency guarantees a similar improvement in productivity" is FALSE: efficiency is the narrower concept, and improving it does not necessarily improve overall productivity.

terms.short: An estimate about the future value of a variable, such as demand; it reduces some of the uncertainty in planning but does not eliminate it.
terms.more: Forecasts are a basic input in operations decisions because they provide information on future demand, and the primary goal of operations management is to match supply to demand.

terms.short: Forecasts based on analysis of subjective inputs from consumer surveys, sales staff, managers and executives, and panels of experts.
terms.more: One of three classifications of techniques: judgmental, time-series, associative. Qualitative methods permit soft information (human factors, opinions, hunches) but risk personal bias.

confusedWith.note: quantitative; project past data using hard, objective data

terms.trap: "Qualitative methods avoid personal bias" is FALSE: it is quantitative methods that usually avoid personal biases.

terms.short: Forecasts that project past experience into the future, assuming the future will be like the past, without trying to identify causes.
terms.more: Some models smooth out random variations; others identify specific patterns and extrapolate them. They rely strictly on historical data.

confusedWith.note: uses explanatory variables to predict demand

terms.trap: "Time-series models identify the causes of patterns" is FALSE: associative models use explanatory variables; time-series models make no attempt to identify causes.

terms.short: A forecasting technique that uses equations with one or more explanatory variables to predict demand.
terms.more: Example: paint demand related to price per gallon, advertising spend, drying time, and ease of cleanup. Associative techniques explicitly identify influencing factors; the primary method of analysis is regression.

confusedWith.note: projects past data with no attempt to identify causes

terms.short: An iterative process that circulates a series of anonymous questionnaires among knowledgeable individuals to achieve a consensus forecast.
terms.more: Anonymity encourages honest responses and reduces the risk that one person's opinion will prevail. Useful for technological forecasting and long-term, single-time forecasts, such as predicting when an event will occur.

confusedWith.note: a small group of upper managers meets; one person's view may prevail

terms.trap: "Delphi uses face-to-face group meetings" or "is best for short-term routine forecasts" is FALSE: responses are anonymous questionnaires, mostly for long-term forecasts.

terms.short: A small group of upper-level managers (marketing, operations, finance) meet and collectively develop a forecast, often for long-range planning and new products.
terms.more: Advantage: brings together the managers' knowledge and talents. Disadvantages: one person's view may prevail, and diffused responsibility may mean less pressure to produce a good forecast.

confusedWith.note: anonymous questionnaires reduce the risk that one view prevails

terms.short: Forecasts from sales or customer service staff, who are good sources because of their direct contact with customers.
terms.more: Three drawbacks: they may be unable to distinguish what customers would like to do from what they actually will do; they are sometimes overly influenced by recent experience; and when forecasts set quotas, they benefit from giving low estimates.

confusedWith.note: samples consumers directly; expensive and needs skill

terms.trap: "Salespeople have an incentive to overestimate when forecasts set quotas" is FALSE: the conflict of interest leads them to underestimate.

terms.short: Sampling consumer opinions through surveys, since consumers ultimately determine demand; they tap information not available elsewhere.
terms.more: Disadvantages: they need considerable knowledge and skill, are expensive and time-consuming, must contend with irrational behavior, and low response rates should, but often don't, make results suspect.

confusedWith.note: sales staff estimates based on direct customer contact

terms.short: A time-ordered sequence of observations taken at regular intervals, such as hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, or annually.
terms.more: A demand forecast should be based on a time series of past demand rather than unit sales, because sales understate demand when stockouts occur.
terms.trap: "Demand forecasts should be based on past sales" is FALSE: sales understate demand when demand exceeds sales.

terms.short: A long-term upward or downward movement in time-series data.
terms.more: Caused by things like population shifts, changing incomes, and cultural changes. One of five patterns: trend, seasonality, cycles, irregular variations, random variations.

confusedWith.note: short-term, fairly regular, calendar-related
wavelike variations of more than one year

terms.short: Short-term, fairly regular variations in data generally related to the calendar or time of day.
terms.more: Restaurants, supermarkets, and theaters have weekly and even daily seasonal variations, so seasonality is not only annual.

confusedWith.note: wavelike variations lasting more than one year
long-term upward or downward movement

terms.trap: "Seasonality refers to variations of more than one year" is FALSE: that describes cycles; seasonality is short-term and not only annual.

terms.short: Wavelike variations of more than one year's duration, often two to six years between peaks, related to economic, political, or agricultural conditions.
terms.more: Frequent irregularity makes turning points hard to identify. The most common approach is explanatory: find a leading variable, such as housing starts, that relates to and leads the variable of interest.

confusedWith.note: short-term, calendar or time-of-day related

terms.short: Variation caused by unusual circumstances, such as severe weather, strikes, or a major product change, that does not reflect typical behavior.
terms.more: Irregular variations can distort the picture and should be identified and removed from the data whenever possible.

confusedWith.note: residual variation left after everything else; always present

terms.trap: "Strikes and severe weather cause random variations" is FALSE: unusual circumstances cause irregular variations.

terms.short: Residual variations that remain after all other behaviors in the data have been accounted for; there are always random variations.
terms.more: Also called white noise; it cannot be reliably predicted. A forecast is generally deemed adequate when its errors show only random variation.

confusedWith.note: caused by unusual circumstances; should be removed

terms.short: A forecast that uses a single previous value of a time series as the basis for the next forecast.
terms.more: Virtually no cost, quick, and easy to understand, but its main objection is that it cannot provide highly accurate forecasts. Its accuracy serves as a standard of comparison for other techniques; it does not smooth at all.

confusedWith.note: averages several recent values, which smooths the data

terms.short: A technique that averages a number of the most recent actual values, adding the newest and dropping the oldest as new data arrive.
terms.more: It lags the actual data and is smoother than it. All values are weighted equally. The fewer the data points, the more responsive the average; more periods give more smoothing and greater lag.

confusedWith.note: gives more weight to the most recent values
previous forecast plus a percentage of the error

terms.trap: "Using more periods makes a moving average more responsive" is FALSE: fewer periods make it more responsive.

terms.short: A moving average that typically gives more weight to the most recent values; the weights must sum to 1.00.
terms.more: Advantage over a simple moving average: more reflective of recent occurrences. Disadvantage: the choice of weights is somewhat arbitrary, generally trial and error.

confusedWith.note: weights all values equally

terms.short: A weighted averaging method in which each new forecast equals the previous forecast plus a percentage of the forecast error.
terms.more: One of the most widely used techniques because it is easy to calculate and the weighting is easily changed by altering the smoothing constant. It is appropriate only for data that vary around an average or have step or gradual changes, not trend.

confusedWith.note: adds a trend factor for series with linear trend

terms.trap: "Simple exponential smoothing is appropriate for trended data" is FALSE: on trended data its forecasts lag the trend.

terms.short: In exponential smoothing, alpha: the percentage of the forecast error added to the previous forecast, commonly .05 to .50.
terms.more: Alpha near 0 means slower adjustment and more smoothing; alpha near 1.00 means more responsiveness and less smoothing. Use a low alpha when the underlying average is stable and a higher alpha when it is susceptible to change.
terms.trap: "A smoothing constant closer to 0 gives greater responsiveness" is FALSE: that reverses it; a low alpha gives more smoothing and slower adjustment.

terms.short: Forecasting based on best recent performance: several methods are tried on recent data and the most accurate one makes next month's forecast.
terms.more: Developed by Bernard T. Smith. Done for each product or service and repeated monthly, using the last few months of data with irregular variations removed.

confusedWith.note: for new products, based on adoption rates, media, word of mouth

terms.short: Models for new products or services without historical data, based on rates of product adoption and usage spread from established products.
terms.more: Factors include market potential, attention from mass media, and word of mouth. Widely used in marketing and to assess investing in new technologies.

confusedWith.note: picks the best-performing recent method each month

terms.short: A linear equation, F = a + bt, used to develop forecasts when trend is present; a is the intercept and b the slope.
terms.more: Coefficients are found by least squares, the same equations as linear regression with t replacing x. Trend projections are much simpler with a trend line, and trend equations can project over much longer periods than smoothing.

confusedWith.note: can adjust to changes in trend

terms.short: A variation of exponential smoothing, also called double smoothing, used when a time series exhibits a linear trend.
terms.more: The forecast has two elements, a smoothed error (S) and a trend factor (T), using alpha (smoothing constant for the average) and beta (smoothing constant for trend). Unlike a linear trend line, it can adjust to changes in trend.

confusedWith.note: simple version; lags trended data
simpler projections but cannot adjust to trend changes

terms.trap: "Beta is the smoothing constant for the average" is FALSE: alpha smooths the average and beta smooths the trend.

terms.short: Regularly repeating upward or downward movements in series values that can be tied to recurring events.
terms.more: May be annual (weather, holidays) but also daily, weekly, or monthly, such as rush hour twice a day. Two models: additive (seasonality as a quantity) and multiplicative (as a percentage, much more widely used).

terms.short: A seasonal index in the multiplicative model: the season's value expressed as a percentage of the average or trend, such as 1.20.
terms.more: Two uses: deseasonalize data by dividing each data point by its relative, and incorporate seasonality by multiplying the trend estimate by the relative. Computed by the centered moving average method or the simple average method.
terms.trap: "To deseasonalize data, multiply by the seasonal relative" is FALSE: deseasonalize by dividing; multiply to incorporate seasonality.

terms.short: A moving average positioned at the center of the data used to compute it; a widely used method for computing seasonal relatives.
terms.more: It accounts for any trend (linear or curvilinear) and is accepted as accurate, but manual computation is cumbersome. A centered moving average with length equal to the season length eliminates seasonality.

confusedWith.note: simpler; works with a stationary mean; not for data with trend

terms.short: A way to compute seasonal relatives: each relative is the average for that season divided by the average of all seasons.
terms.more: Its advantage is simplicity, and it works well when data have a stationary mean. Conventional wisdom says not to use it when linear trend is present.

confusedWith.note: accounts for trend; accurate but cumbersome

terms.short: A technique for fitting a line to a set of points; the primary method of analysis in associative forecasting.
terms.more: Three weaknesses: simple linear regression applies only to linear relationships with one independent variable; it needs considerable data (20 or more observations); and all observations are weighted equally.
terms.trap: "Regression weights recent observations more heavily" is FALSE: all observations are weighted equally.

terms.short: The explanatory (independent) variables that can be used to predict values of the variable of interest.
terms.more: Examples: beef sales related to beef price and the prices of chicken, pork, and lamb. The predictor goes on the x-axis and the predicted variable on the y-axis.
terms.trap: "x is the dependent variable" is FALSE: x is the predictor (independent) variable; y is the predicted variable.

terms.short: The straight line that minimizes the sum of squared vertical deviations of the data points from the line.
terms.more: Written y = a + bx, where b is the slope and a is the value of y when x = 0. It should be used only for the range of values from which it was developed.
terms.trap: "Least squares minimizes horizontal deviations or the plain sum of deviations" is FALSE: it minimizes the sum of squared vertical deviations.

terms.short: A measure of the scatter of data points around a regression line; points closer to the line mean more accurate predictions.

confusedWith.note: MSE and its square root measure forecast error spread and set control limits

terms.short: A measure of the strength and direction of a relationship between two variables; the coefficient r ranges from -1.00 to +1.00.
terms.more: +1.00 means changes always move together in the same direction; -1.00 means increases in one are matched by decreases in the other; near zero means little linear relationship.

confusedWith.note: r squared; 0 to 1; percent of variation explained

terms.trap: "r ranges from 0 to 1" or "r near 0 means a strong negative relationship" is FALSE: r runs from -1 to +1, and near 0 means little linear relationship.

terms.short: r squared: the percentage of variability in y explained by the independent variable, ranging from 0 to 1.00.
terms.more: r squared of .80 or more indicates a good predictor, .25 or less a poor one, and between them a moderate one.

confusedWith.note: r; -1 to +1; strength and direction

terms.trap: "r squared ranges from -1 to +1" is FALSE: it ranges from 0 to 1.00.

terms.short: The difference between the actual value and the value that was predicted for a given period: Actual minus Forecast.
terms.more: A positive error means the forecast was too low; a negative error means it was too high. Errors influence decisions in two ways: choosing between forecasting alternatives and evaluating a technique in use.
terms.trap: "A positive error means the forecast was too high" is FALSE: error is actual minus forecast, so positive means the forecast was too low.

terms.short: Mean absolute deviation: the average absolute forecast error, which weights all errors evenly (linearly) and is easiest to compute.

confusedWith.note: squares errors, giving more weight to large errors
relative error; compares across different scales

terms.trap: "MAD gives more weight to larger errors" is FALSE: that is MSE; MAD weights errors linearly.

terms.short: Mean squared error: the average of squared forecast errors, which gives more weight to larger errors.
terms.more: Larger errors typically cause more problems. The square root of MSE estimates the standard deviation of errors and is used to set control-chart limits.

confusedWith.note: weights errors linearly; easiest to compute
weights errors by relative size

terms.trap: "MSE is the easiest measure to compute" is FALSE: that is MAD.

terms.short: Mean absolute percent error: the average absolute percent error, which weights errors according to their relative size.
terms.more: Used to put errors in perspective (an error of 10 on 15 is huge, on 10,000 insignificant) and to compare forecast errors across different products or services.

confusedWith.note: absolute errors weighted linearly
squared errors

terms.trap: "Use MAD to compare errors across products of different scale" is FALSE: that is what MAPE is for.

terms.short: A visual tool for monitoring forecast errors that plots them in order against a center line of zero and upper and lower control limits.
terms.more: Errors are in control only if all are within the limits and show no patterns. It judges every error individually and is generally superior to the tracking signal.

confusedWith.note: cumulative error divided by MAD; errors can cancel

terms.trap: "Errors are in control as long as all are within the limits" is FALSE: there must also be no patterns.

terms.short: A persistent tendency for forecasts to be greater or less than the actual values of a time series.
terms.more: Detected by the tracking signal; a large average error also suggests a biased forecast.

terms.short: The ratio of cumulative forecast error to MAD, used to detect bias in forecast errors over time.
terms.more: Zero is ideal; limits of plus or minus 4 or 5 are often used. Its weakness is using cumulative errors, so large positive and negative errors can cancel each other out.

confusedWith.note: judges each error individually; generally superior

terms.trap: "The tracking signal is superior because it uses cumulative errors" is FALSE: cumulative errors can cancel, so the control chart is generally superior; the ideal value is zero, not 1.

terms.short: Viewing forecasts as probable future demand and reacting to meet it by adjusting production rates, inventories, and workforce.

confusedWith.note: actively influences demand

terms.trap: "The reactive approach seeks to actively influence demand" is FALSE: that is the proactive approach; the reactive approach reacts to meet forecast demand.

terms.short: Seeking to actively influence demand through advertising, pricing, or product and service changes.
terms.more: Generally requires an explanatory model, such as regression, or a subjective assessment of the influence on demand.

confusedWith.note: reacts to meet forecast demand

terms.trap: "The proactive approach views forecasts as probable future demand and reacts to meet it" is FALSE: that is the reactive approach; the proactive approach tries to influence demand.

terms.short: The seven requirements a good forecast should meet, from timely and accurate to cost-effective.
terms.more: Seven: timely; accurate, with the degree of accuracy stated; reliable; expressed in meaningful units; in writing; technique simple to understand and use; cost-effective.
terms.trap: "A good forecast should use the most sophisticated technique available" is FALSE: the technique should be simple to understand and use.

terms.short: Six steps in order, from determining the forecast's purpose through monitoring the forecast errors.
terms.more: Six: determine the purpose; establish a time horizon; obtain, clean, and analyze data; select a technique; make the forecast; monitor the forecast errors. Once set up, only steps 3 and 6 may need repeating.
terms.trap: "Once set up, only steps 4 and 5 need repeating" is FALSE: it is steps 3 and 6.

terms.short: The upper limit or ceiling on the load that an operating unit can handle.
terms.more: Load can be physical units produced or services performed; an operating unit can be a plant, department, machine, store, or worker. Capacity needs include equipment, space, and employee skills.

terms.short: Excess capacity beyond what demand requires, which leads to operating costs that are too high.

confusedWith.note: too little capacity: strained resources and possible loss of customers

terms.trap: "Overcapacity causes strained resources and loss of customers" is FALSE: that's undercapacity; overcapacity means operating costs that are too high.

terms.short: Too little capacity for demand, which leads to strained resources and possible loss of customers.

confusedWith.note: excess capacity: operating costs that are too high

terms.trap: "Undercapacity causes operating costs that are too high" is FALSE: that's overcapacity; undercapacity strains resources and may lose customers.

terms.term: Three key questions in capacity planning
terms.short: What kind of capacity is needed, how much is needed to match demand, and when is it needed.
terms.more: Exactly three questions. Forecasts are key inputs for how much and when; the kind of capacity depends on the products and services offered and on operations strategy.
terms.trap: "Forecasts answer what kind of capacity is needed" is FALSE: forecasts answer how much and when.

terms.short: The maximum output rate or service capacity an operation, process, or facility is designed for, achieved under ideal conditions.
terms.more: Hierarchy: actual output is at most effective capacity, which is less than design capacity.

confusedWith.note: design capacity minus allowances such as personal time and preventive maintenance
what is actually produced; cannot exceed effective capacity

terms.short: Design capacity minus allowances such as personal time and preventive maintenance; always less than design capacity.
terms.more: Reduced by planned allowances: changing product mix, periodic maintenance, lunch and coffee breaks, and problems in scheduling and balancing operations. It acts as a lid on actual output, so increasing it is the real key to improving utilization.

confusedWith.note: the maximum under ideal conditions
reduced below effective capacity by unplanned problems like breakdowns and absenteeism

terms.trap: "Effective capacity can exceed design capacity" is FALSE: effective capacity is always less than design capacity.

terms.short: The output actually achieved; it cannot exceed effective capacity and is often less.
terms.more: Reduced by unplanned factors: machine breakdowns, absenteeism, shortages of materials, quality problems, and factors outside operations managers' control.

confusedWith.note: reduced by planned allowances such as breaks, maintenance, and product mix
the maximum under ideal conditions

terms.trap: "Actual output can exceed effective capacity" is FALSE: actual output cannot exceed effective capacity.

terms.short: The ratio of actual output to effective capacity, expressed as a percentage.
terms.more: Focusing exclusively on efficiency can be misleading when effective capacity is low relative to design capacity; utilization is probably more meaningful.

confusedWith.note: actual output divided by design capacity

terms.trap: "Efficiency is actual output divided by design capacity" is FALSE: that's utilization; efficiency divides by effective capacity.

terms.short: The ratio of actual output to design capacity, expressed as a percentage.
terms.more: Benefits of high utilization are realized only when there is demand for the output; otherwise excess output adds variable and inventory carrying costs. To raise utilization, increase effective capacity.

confusedWith.note: actual output divided by effective capacity

terms.trap: "Higher utilization is always better" is FALSE: without demand for the output, focusing on utilization is counterproductive.

terms.short: The eight categories of factors that affect effective capacity.
terms.more: Exactly eight: facilities, products and services, processes, human considerations, policy factors, operational factors, supply chain, and external forces.
terms.trap: "Unions and safety regulations are human factors" is FALSE: they are external factors.

terms.short: Building capacity in anticipation of future demand increases.
terms.more: If capacity increases involve a long lead time, this may be the best option. Similar to the expand-early strategy.

confusedWith.note: builds capacity when demand exceeds current capacity
adds capacity in relatively small increments

terms.trap: "Leading is best when lead times are short" is FALSE: leading may be best when capacity increases involve a long lead time.

terms.short: Building capacity when demand exceeds current capacity.
terms.more: Similar to the wait-and-see strategy.

confusedWith.note: builds capacity in anticipation of demand
like following, but in relatively small increments

terms.trap: "Following builds capacity ahead of demand" is FALSE: that's leading; following builds when demand exceeds capacity.

terms.short: Similar to following, but adding capacity in relatively small increments to keep pace with increasing demand.

confusedWith.note: builds capacity when demand exceeds current capacity
builds capacity in anticipation of demand

terms.trap: "Tracking adds capacity in large chunks" is FALSE: tracking adds relatively small increments.

terms.short: An amount of capacity in excess of expected demand when demand is uncertain; capacity minus expected demand.
terms.more: Greater demand uncertainty calls for a greater cushion; standard products and services generally need smaller cushions. A cushion may provide flexibility at added cost, or block market entry.
terms.trap: "Capacity cushion is capacity divided by expected demand" is FALSE: it is capacity minus expected demand. Also, more uncertainty means a larger cushion, not a smaller one.

terms.term: Steps in the capacity planning process
terms.short: Eight steps from estimating future capacity requirements through monitoring results.
terms.more: In order: estimate future requirements; evaluate existing capacity and identify gaps; identify alternatives; conduct financial analyses; assess key qualitative issues; select the best long-term alternative; implement it; monitor results.

terms.short: Considerations about the overall level of capacity, such as facility size.

confusedWith.note: probable variations from seasonal, random, and irregular fluctuations

terms.trap: "Long-term considerations relate to probable variations in capacity requirements" is FALSE: that's short-term.

terms.short: Considerations about probable variations in capacity requirements from seasonal, random, and irregular fluctuations.
terms.more: Irregular variations are perhaps the most troublesome because they are difficult or impossible to predict.

confusedWith.note: the overall level of capacity, such as facility size

terms.section: 5.7 Additional Challenges of Planning Service Capacity
terms.short: Three very important factors: the need to be near customers, the inability to store services, and the degree of volatility of demand.
terms.more: Capacity and location are closely tied for services; demand volatility is higher for services than goods, and services cannot use inventory to smooth demand.
terms.trap: "Services can be inventoried to smooth demand" is FALSE: services cannot be stored.

terms.short: An operation in a sequence whose capacity is lower than the others', so its capacity limits system capacity.
terms.more: A bottleneck is evidence of an unbalanced system. Raising the bottleneck helps only until the next-lowest operation becomes the limit.

confusedWith.note: anything limiting performance: market, resource, material, financial, supplier, knowledge, or policy

terms.trap: "Increasing a non-bottleneck operation increases system output" is FALSE: system capacity is limited to the bottleneck's capacity.

terms.short: Products or services whose demand patterns offset each other, ideally using the same resources at different times.
terms.more: Examples: snow skis and water skis; heating and air-conditioning equipment. Result: stable overall capacity requirements and minimized inventory.

terms.short: When output is below the optimal level, increasing output decreases average unit costs.
terms.more: Three reasons: fixed costs are spread over more units; construction costs increase at a decreasing rate with facility size; processing costs decrease as operations become more standardized.

confusedWith.note: beyond the optimal level, average unit costs increase

terms.trap: "Economies of scale is when average cost per unit increases as volume increases" is FALSE: unit cost decreases.

terms.short: When output is increased beyond the optimal level, average unit costs increase.
terms.more: Four reasons: distribution costs rise (traffic congestion, shipping from one large centralized facility); complexity increases costs; inflexibility; additional levels of bureaucracy.

confusedWith.note: below the optimal level, more output lowers unit cost

terms.trap: "Diseconomies of scale occur when costs decrease past optimal capacity" is FALSE: costs increase.

terms.short: The output level at which a production unit's cost per unit is lowest.
terms.more: The cost curve is U-shaped. Larger plants tend to have higher optimal output rates and lower minimum costs than smaller plants.

terms.short: Something that limits the performance of a process or system in achieving its goals.
terms.more: Seven categories: market, resource, material, financial, supplier, knowledge or competency, and policy. Based on Eli Goldratt (The Theory of Constraints) and Eli Schragenheim and H. William Dettmer (Manufacturing at Warp Speed).

confusedWith.note: specifically the lowest-capacity operation in a sequence

terms.trap: "Adding resources at non-bottleneck operations increases system capacity" is FALSE: capacity increases only by loosening the constraints.

terms.term: Five steps to resolve constraint issues
terms.short: Identify the most pressing constraint, change the operation for maximum benefit given it, make other portions supportive, find ways to overcome it, and repeat.
terms.more: In order: identify the most pressing constraint; change the operation to achieve maximum benefit given the constraint; make sure other portions of the process support the constraint; explore and evaluate ways to overcome it; repeat until the level of constraints is acceptable.
terms.trap: "The first step is to overcome all constraints simultaneously" is FALSE: the first step is to identify the most pressing constraint.

terms.short: Analysis of the relationships between cost, revenue, and volume of output to estimate income under different operating conditions.
terms.more: Six assumptions: one product; everything produced can be sold; variable cost per unit is constant; fixed costs are constant or step changes; revenue per unit is constant; revenue per unit exceeds variable cost per unit.
terms.trap: "Cost-volume analysis assumes multiple products with different costs" is FALSE: it assumes one product, and that everything produced can be sold.

terms.short: Costs that tend to remain constant regardless of volume of output.
terms.more: Examples: rent, property taxes, equipment costs, heating and cooling, certain administrative costs.

confusedWith.note: vary directly with volume
increase stepwise as potential volume increases

terms.short: Costs that vary directly with volume of output, mainly materials and labor.

confusedWith.note: remain constant regardless of volume
increase stepwise as potential volume increases

terms.short: Costs that increase stepwise as potential volume increases, such as buying one, two, or three machines.
terms.more: Step costs can produce multiple break-even quantities, and some ranges may have no break-even point.

confusedWith.note: remain constant regardless of volume
vary directly with volume

terms.short: Revenue per unit minus variable cost per unit.
The volume of output at which total cost equals total revenue.
terms.more: Below the BEP there is a loss; above it, a profit.

confusedWith.note: where two competing alternatives are equal

terms.short: The quantity at which a decision maker is indifferent between two competing alternatives.
terms.more: It is where the two alternatives' profit or cost lines intersect.

confusedWith.note: where total cost equals total revenue

terms.short: The difference between cash received from sales and other sources and cash outflow for labor, materials, overhead, and taxes.

confusedWith.note: the current value of all future cash flows

terms.short: The sum, in current value, of all future cash flows of an investment proposal.
terms.more: The present value method accounts for the time value of money, summarizing initial cost, annual cash flows, and salvage value in a single equivalent current value.

confusedWith.note: cash in minus cash out
ignores the time value of money
expressed as an equivalent interest rate, not a dollar value

terms.short: The length of time for an investment to return its original cost; crude but widely used.
terms.more: It does not take into account the time value of money and is easier to rationalize for short-term paybacks.

confusedWith.note: accounts for the time value of money
an equivalent interest rate

terms.trap: "Payback accounts for the time value of money" is FALSE: payback ignores it.

terms.short: The rate of return that equates estimated future returns and initial cost.
terms.more: It summarizes initial cost, expected annual cash flows, and salvage value in an equivalent interest rate.

confusedWith.note: a single equivalent current (dollar) value
time to return original cost; ignores time value of money

terms.trap: "IRR expresses results as a dollar value" is FALSE: present value does; IRR is a rate.

terms.short: A method for financially comparing alternatives under conditions of risk or uncertainty.
terms.more: It identifies possible future conditions, lists alternatives, and develops a payoff for each combination. Payback, present value, and IRR are appropriate when there is a high degree of certainty; under risk or uncertainty, decision theory is used.

terms.short: Expanding capacity before demand materializes, to gain economies of scale, expand market share, and preempt competitors.
terms.more: Risks: oversupply driving prices down, and underutilized equipment raising unit costs. Roughly corresponds to the leading strategy.

confusedWith.note: expands only after demand materializes; risks losing market share

terms.trap: "Expand-early offers a lower chance of oversupply and higher capacity utilization" is FALSE: those are wait-and-see advantages; expand-early risks oversupply and underutilized equipment.

terms.short: Expanding capacity only after demand materializes, perhaps incrementally.
terms.more: Advantages: lower chance of oversupply and higher capacity utilization. Risks: loss of market share and inability to meet demand if expansion has a long lead time or demand rises unexpectedly.

confusedWith.note: expands before demand; risks oversupply and underutilization

terms.trap: "Wait-and-see risks oversupply" is FALSE: its risks are losing market share and being unable to meet demand.

terms.section: 6.1 Introduction to Process Selection and Facility Layout
terms.short: Deciding on the way production of goods or services will be organized.
terms.more: It has major implications for capacity planning, layout of facilities, equipment, and design of work systems. Except for projects, it is usually a function of the volume and variety needed.

confusedWith.note: layout is the configuration of departments, work centers, and equipment; process type and layout are closely related

terms.section: 6.1 Introduction to Process Selection and Facility Layout
terms.short: The mix of equipment and labor the organization will use; a key aspect of process strategy.

confusedWith.note: the degree to which the system can adjust to changes in processing requirements

terms.section: 6.1 Introduction to Process Selection and Facility Layout
terms.short: The degree to which the system can adjust to changes in processing requirements, such as changes in design, volume processed, or technology.
terms.more: Flexible systems are often more expensive and less efficient. They are chosen when demand variety exists or when demand is uncertain (the latter can be overcome through improved forecasting).

confusedWith.note: the mix of equipment and labor the organization will use

terms.trap: "Flexibility is always the best processing choice" is FALSE: flexibility should be adopted with great care, only where the need clearly exists.

terms.section: Five basic process types: job shop, batch, repetitive, continuous, project
terms.short: A small-scale, intermittent process for low volumes of high-variety work, using general-purpose equipment and skilled workers.
terms.more: Examples: a tool-and-die shop, a veterinarian's office. Low fixed costs, high variable costs, high cost per unit, complex scheduling, high work-in-process inventory.

confusedWith.note: moderate volume and variety, less flexible equipment, lower worker skill
high volume of standardized output, low worker skill

terms.trap: "Job shops have high fixed costs" is FALSE: job shops have low fixed costs and high variable costs.

terms.section: Five basic process types: job shop, batch, repetitive, continuous, project
terms.short: A process for moderate volume and moderate variety; processing is still intermittent, but equipment need not be as flexible, and worker skill not as high, as in a job shop.
terms.more: Examples: bakeries, movie theaters (batches of people), airlines (planeloads). Work-in-process inventory is high.

confusedWith.note: low volume, high variety, general-purpose equipment, skilled workers

terms.trap: "Batch processing has low work-in-process inventory" is FALSE: batch WIP is high.

terms.section: Five basic process types: job shop, batch, repetitive, continuous, project
terms.short: A process for higher volumes of more standardized goods or services, using production and assembly lines, slightly flexible equipment, and generally low-skilled workers.
