terms.more: Examples: automobiles, smartphones, an automatic carwash, cafeteria lines. Uses special-purpose equipment; low unit cost but low flexibility and high cost of downtime. Mass customization falls into this category.

confusedWith.note: very high volume of nondiscrete, highly standardized output

terms.trap: "Repetitive processing uses general-purpose equipment" is FALSE: it uses special-purpose equipment.

terms.section: Five basic process types: job shop, batch, repetitive, continuous, project
terms.short: A process for very high volumes of nondiscrete, highly standardized output, with almost no variety and so no need for equipment flexibility.
terms.more: Examples: petroleum products, steel, sugar, salt, electricity supply. Worker skill ranges from low to high; very high fixed costs, very low variable costs, very rigid, very high cost of downtime.

confusedWith.note: higher volumes of more standardized goods or services on production or assembly lines

terms.trap: "Continuous processing has high variable costs" is FALSE: its variable costs are very low.

terms.section: Five basic process types: job shop, batch, repetitive, continuous, project
terms.short: A process for nonroutine work with a unique set of objectives to be accomplished in a limited time frame.
terms.more: Examples: putting on a play, making a motion picture, building a dam or bridge. Unlike the other four ongoing types, projects are of limited duration; equipment flexibility and worker skills range from low to high, and they use fixed-position layouts.

terms.section: Five basic process types: job shop, batch, repetitive, continuous, project
terms.short: A repetitive approach that uses modular product and process designs while letting customer specifications directly influence final characteristics.
terms.more: It delays differentiation, gaining economies of scale from standardization before customizing.

confusedWith.note: holding products in standardized form until a demand signal triggers finishing
standardized subprocesses that can be quickly reconfigured

terms.trap: "Mass customization falls into the job shop category" is FALSE: it falls into the repetitive category.

terms.section: Five basic process types: job shop, batch, repetitive, continuous, project
terms.short: Using standardized subprocesses that can be quickly reconfigured to respond to unplanned customer needs.
terms.more: Examples: a gas pump blending mid-range octane, customizable soda machines, fast casual restaurants like Five Guys and Moe's.

confusedWith.note: the overall repetitive approach using modular designs and customer specifications
holding products in standardized form until demand triggers finishing

terms.section: Five basic process types: job shop, batch, repetitive, continuous, project
terms.short: Holding unfinished products or services in standardized form until a demand signal triggers subprocesses to finish them into customized form.

confusedWith.note: the overall repetitive approach using modular designs and customer specifications
standardized subprocesses that can be quickly reconfigured

terms.short: Identifying key product or service dimensions and then selecting appropriate processes, to avoid mismatches between operations capabilities and market conditions.
terms.more: Key dimensions: range of products or services processed, expected order sizes, pricing strategies, expected frequency of schedule changes, and order-winning requirements.

terms.short: The discovery and development of new or improved products, services, or processes for producing or providing them.
Machinery that has sensing and control devices that enable it to operate without human interference.
terms.more: Advantages: low variability and reduced variable costs. Limitations: costly (usually needs high volumes), much less flexible than human labor, and workers' fear of job loss. Job requirements must be standardized for automation to be an option.
terms.trap: "Automate first, then remove waste" is FALSE: remove waste from the system before automating, to avoid building waste into the automated system.

terms.short: The least flexible kind of automation: high-cost, specialized equipment for a fixed sequence of operations.
terms.more: Advantages: low cost and high volume. Limitations: minimal variety and high cost of major changes in product or process.

confusedWith.note: general-purpose, computer-programmed equipment for low-volume variety in small batches
less changeover time; variety without batches

terms.trap: "Fixed automation is the most flexible" is FALSE: it is the least flexible.

terms.short: High-cost, general-purpose equipment controlled by a computer program, able to economically produce a fairly wide variety of low-volume products in small batches.
terms.more: N/C machines and some robots are applications.

confusedWith.note: least flexible; specialized equipment, fixed sequence, high volume
evolved from programmable; significantly less changeover time

terms.trap: "Programmable automation is best for high volume, low variety" is FALSE: it suits a fairly wide variety of low-volume products in small batches.

terms.short: Automation evolved from programmable automation, using more customized equipment that requires significantly less changeover time, giving variety without producing in batches.

confusedWith.note: general-purpose equipment producing low-volume variety in small batches
least flexible; fixed sequence

terms.trap: "Flexible automation requires more changeover time than programmable automation" is FALSE: it requires significantly less.

terms.short: Machines programmed to follow processing instructions based on mathematical relationships.
terms.more: Best used for frequent small batches, complex geometry, close tolerances, costly mistakes, and frequent design changes. Main limitations: higher skill needed to program, and inability to detect tool wear and material variation.

confusedWith.note: an individual N/C machine with its own computer

terms.short: An individual machine tool with its own computer that reads instructions, created by CAM software, and drives the tool.
terms.more: One computer controlling several N/C machines is instead direct numerical control (DNC). CNC controllers have dramatically increased job shop production.

confusedWith.note: the general category of machines following mathematical instructions

terms.short: The use of computers in process control, ranging from robots to automated quality control.

confusedWith.note: links design, FMSs, purchasing, order processing, and production planning and control

terms.short: Robots designed to work collaboratively and safely with humans, augmenting human capabilities and stopping or reversing on contact with a person.

confusedWith.note: do heavy or dirty work, at levels from fixed instructions up to simple decisions

terms.short: A group of machines with supervisory computer control, automatic material handling, and robots or other automated processing equipment.
terms.more: Produces a variety of similar products, needing lower capital investment and giving higher flexibility than fixed automation. Limited to a relatively narrow range of part variety (a family of similar parts); FMSs are more fully automated versions of cellular manufacturing.

confusedWith.note: a broader system linking design, FMSs, purchasing, order processing, and production planning

terms.short: A system linking a broad range of manufacturing activities: engineering design, FMSs, purchasing, order processing, and production planning and control.
terms.more: Overall goal: rapid response to customer orders and/or product changes, rapid production, and reduced indirect labor costs. Example: Allen-Bradley's factory within a factory.

confusedWith.note: a group of machines under supervisory computer control
computers used in process control

terms.short: Additive manufacturing: creating three-dimensional objects by applying successive layers of material, using an industrial robot controlled by CAD.
terms.more: It contrasts with subtractive manufacturing (cutting, grinding, drilling, milling). It is generally much slower than conventional factory techniques and unlikely to replace high-volume production.

confusedWith.note: material removed by cutting, grinding, sanding, drilling, milling

terms.trap: "3D printing is subtractive, or faster than conventional mass production" is FALSE: it is additive and generally much slower.

terms.short: The configuration of departments, work centers, and equipment, with particular emphasis on movement of work (customers or materials) through the system.
terms.more: Layout decisions matter for 3 reasons: substantial investments of money and effort, long-term commitments, and significant impact on cost and efficiency. The basic objective is a smooth flow of work, material, and information.

confusedWith.note: deciding how production will be organized

terms.trap: "Layout decisions involve short-term commitments" is FALSE: they involve long-term commitments, making mistakes difficult to overcome.

terms.short: A layout for repetitive processing that achieves a smooth, rapid flow of large volumes, with equipment arranged in the product's processing sequence.
terms.more: Uses fixed-path material handling; high utilization, low unit cost, wide span of supervision. But it is inflexible, highly vulnerable to shutdowns, has dull jobs, and makes individual incentive plans impractical.

confusedWith.note: intermittent processing, variable-path handling, less vulnerable to breakdowns, individual incentives possible

terms.trap: "Product layouts are less vulnerable to breakdowns" is FALSE: their interdependent workstations make them highly vulnerable to shutdowns.

terms.short: A standardized layout for repetitive processing in which every item follows the same sequence, typically moved by fixed-path equipment such as conveyors.

confusedWith.note: a line for the last stages of an assembled product

terms.section: Five basic process types: job shop, batch, repetitive, continuous, project
terms.short: A standardized repetitive-processing line covering the last stages of producing an assembled product.

confusedWith.note: the general standardized line for repetitive processing

terms.short: A functional layout that groups similar activities into departments, handling a variety of processing requirements with general-purpose equipment.
terms.more: Less susceptible to breakdowns and allows individual incentives, but needs continual routing and scheduling and variable-path material handling. WIP is high, equipment utilization is low (often under 50%), and output rates are much lower than product layouts.

confusedWith.note: repetitive processing, fixed-path handling, high utilization, highly vulnerable to breakdowns

terms.trap: "Process layouts have higher equipment utilization" is FALSE: their utilization rates are low.

terms.short: Non-continuous work flow caused by frequent equipment adjustments to handle a variety of processing requirements; served by process layouts.
A layout where the item being worked on stays stationary and workers, materials, and equipment are moved to it as needed.
terms.more: Used for projects when weight, size, or bulk make moving the product impractical: buildings, dams, shipbuilding, large aircraft. Span of control can be narrow, so the administrative burden is often higher than other layouts.

terms.short: A layout grouping workstations into cells based on the operations needed for a set of similar items, or part families, requiring similar processing.
terms.more: Cells are miniature versions of product layouts in which all parts follow the same route. Compared with functional layouts: fewer moves, shorter travel, fixed paths, lower WIP and throughput time, higher equipment utilization.

confusedWith.note: identifying and grouping items into part families
a more fully automated version of cellular manufacturing

terms.short: Shigeo Shingo's method for cutting changeover time by converting internal activities to external ones, then streamlining the remaining internal activities.
terms.more: Internal activities can only be done while the machine is stopped; external ones are done before or after without stopping it. In 1982 Toyota cut a changeover from 100 minutes to 3.
terms.trap: "SMED converts external activities to internal" is FALSE: it converts internal to external, and it was developed by Shingo, not Ohno or Deming.

terms.short: Identifying items with similar design or manufacturing characteristics and grouping them into part families.
terms.more: Three primary methods: visual inspection (least accurate, least costly, simplest); examination of design and production data (more accurate, more time-consuming, perhaps most common); production flow analysis (manufacturing perspective, takes existing routings as givens).

confusedWith.note: the layout of workstations into cells

terms.trap: "Visual inspection is the most accurate method" is FALSE: it is the least accurate (though least costly and simplest); and production flow analysis takes a manufacturing, not design, perspective.

terms.short: Assigning tasks to workstations so that task groupings have approximately equal time requirements, minimizing idle time.
terms.more: 3 obstacles to perfect balance: task bundles of equal duration are hard to form, elemental task lengths differ, and required technological sequences prohibit some combinations. Lines with human tasks are rarely perfectly balanced.

terms.short: The maximum time allowed at each workstation to perform its assigned tasks before the work moves on; it sets the line's output rate.
terms.more: Minimum cycle time equals the longest task time; maximum cycle time equals the sum of task times.
terms.trap: "Longer cycle time gives higher output" is FALSE: a longer cycle time means a lower output rate (and minimum cycle time is the longest task, not the sum of task times).

terms.short: A diagram showing the tasks and their sequential (precedence) requirements, read left to right from initial to final task.
The sum of a task's time and the times of all following tasks; one heuristic assigns tasks in order of greatest positional weight.

confusedWith.note: the other heuristic: assign tasks in order of most following tasks

terms.short: The percentage of idle time of a line; efficiency equals 100 percent minus this percentage.

confusedWith.note: 100 percent minus the percentage of idle time

terms.section: Other Approaches to smoothing production flow
terms.short: Cross-training workers so those with temporary idle time can help overburdened workers; used most often in lean production systems.

confusedWith.note: duplicate stations for bottleneck operations
one line handling more than one similar product

terms.section: Other Approaches to smoothing production flow
terms.short: A line designed to handle more than one product, which must be fairly similar, giving great flexibility in varying the output mix.
terms.more: Example: BMW's Dingolfing line produces multiple models without the costly changeovers of single-model lines.

confusedWith.note: cross-training workers to help overburdened stations

terms.short: Richard Muther's approach to process layout using subjective ratings of how important closeness is for each department pair.
terms.more: Ratings: A absolutely necessary, E especially important, I important, O ordinary closeness OK, U unimportant, X undesirable. Critical (A and X) departments are assigned first; it allows multiple objectives, but subjective inputs are imprecise and unreliable.

confusedWith.note: transportation-cost minimization, focusing on a single objective

terms.trap: "Only side-to-side counts as adjacent" is FALSE: departments are close when they touch side to side or corner to corner.

terms.short: Specifying the content and methods of jobs: what will be done, who will do it, how, and where.
terms.more: Its three objectives are productivity, safety, and quality of work life. Job design determines job content; methods analysis determines how a job is done; work measurement determines how long it should take.

confusedWith.note: focuses on how a job is done
studies the human motions used to perform an operation
determines how long a job should take

terms.trap: "Methods analysis determines job content and job design determines how long a job should take" is FALSE: job design is content, methods analysis is how, work measurement is how long.

terms.short: The systematic, logical school of job design; a refinement of Frederick Winslow Taylor's scientific management.
terms.more: One of the two basic schools of thought in job design. Specialization is a primary issue of disagreement between it and the behavioral school.

confusedWith.note: emphasizes satisfaction of wants and needs

terms.short: The school of job design that emphasizes satisfaction of wants and needs; it followed the efficiency approach.
terms.more: One of the two basic schools of thought in job design; it continues to make inroads.

confusedWith.note: systematic, logical; a refinement of Taylor's scientific management

terms.trap: "The behavioral school is a refinement of Taylor's scientific management" is FALSE: that's the efficiency school.

terms.short: Work that concentrates on some aspect of a product or service; jobs with a very narrow scope.
terms.more: Advantages for management: simplified training, high productivity, low wage costs. Advantages for employees: low education and skill requirements, minimum responsibilities, little mental effort. Lower-level specialized jobs are often monotonous, leading to dissatisfaction, turnover, and absenteeism.
terms.trap: "Low wage costs is an advantage of specialization for employees" is FALSE: it's an advantage for management.

terms.short: Giving a worker a larger portion of the total task; horizontal loading at the same level of skill and responsibility.
terms.more: Aims to make jobs more interesting through increased variety of skills and a more recognizable contribution. Used in lean operations along with job enrichment.

confusedWith.note: more responsibility for planning and coordination (vertical loading)
workers periodically exchange jobs

terms.trap: "Job enlargement is vertical loading" is FALSE: enlargement is horizontal loading.

terms.short: Workers periodically exchange jobs, which broadens their learning and lets them fill in for sick or absent workers.

confusedWith.note: a larger portion of the total task (horizontal loading)
more responsibility for planning and coordination (vertical loading)

terms.trap: "Job rotation gives workers more responsibility" is FALSE: that's job enrichment.

terms.short: Increasing a worker's level of responsibility for planning and coordination tasks; vertical loading.
terms.more: Example: supermarket stock clerks handling reordering. Focuses on the motivating potential of worker satisfaction.

confusedWith.note: a larger portion of the total task at the same level (horizontal loading)
workers periodically exchange jobs

terms.trap: "Job enrichment involves giving workers a greater share of the total task" is FALSE: that's enlargement.

terms.short: Long-term teams (self-managed teams) empowered to make certain changes in the work processes under their control.
terms.more: Rationale: workers close to the process know it best and have a vested interest. Benefits: fewer managers needed, improved responsiveness to problems, a personal stake, and less time to implement improvements.

confusedWith.note: collaborate temporarily on quality improvement, design, or problem solving

terms.trap: "Self-directed teams have absolute authority to make all decisions" is FALSE: they are empowered only to change work processes under their control.

terms.short: Teams that collaborate temporarily on quality improvement, product or service design, or problem solving, with members from one or several functional areas.

confusedWith.note: long-term; empowered over their own work processes

terms.term: Robert Bacal's requirements for successful team building
terms.short: Robert Bacal's list of seven requirements a team needs to succeed.
terms.more: The 7: shared vision and goals; talent and skills to meet goals; clear roles and functions; shared procedures and norms; skilled interpersonal relations; a system of reinforcement and celebration; clear relationship to the greater organization.

terms.short: The scientific discipline concerned with interactions between humans and other elements of a system, to optimize human well-being and system performance.
terms.more: The three most common risk factors are awkward postures, excessive force, and repetition. The International Ergonomics Association names three domains: physical, cognitive, and organizational. It applies to office workers too.
terms.trap: "Ergonomics is important for factory workers, but not for office workers" is FALSE: it applies to office workers too, such as computer workstations.

terms.short: The three domains of ergonomics: physical, cognitive, and organizational.
terms.more: Physical: repetitive movements, layout, health, safety. Cognitive: mental workload, decision making, human-computer interaction, work stress. Organizational: communication, teamwork, work design, telework.
terms.trap: "Work stress is physical ergonomics" is FALSE: it is cognitive; likewise telework is organizational, not cognitive.

terms.short: Worker carelessness, one of the two basic causes of accidents, such as failing to use protective equipment or overriding safety controls.
terms.more: Examples: failing to use protective equipment, taping control buttons down, disregarding safety procedures, improper use of tools, failing to use caution in danger zones.

confusedWith.note: accident hazards in the workplace

terms.trap: "Taping control buttons down is an unsafe condition (hazard)" is FALSE: it is an unsafe act.

terms.short: Accident hazards in the workplace, such as unprotected machinery, poorly lit walkways, or uncontained toxic gases.
terms.more: One of the two basic causes of accidents, alongside worker carelessness (unsafe acts).

confusedWith.note: worker carelessness, the other basic cause of accidents

terms.short: Federal agency created by the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 to ensure healthy and safe working conditions in all organizations.
terms.more: It inspects at random and to investigate complaints, and can issue warnings, impose fines, and invoke court-ordered shutdowns. It is a major influence on OM decisions about worker safety.

terms.short: A pay system that compensates employees for the time worked during a pay period; also called hourly and measured daywork systems.
terms.more: More widely used than incentive systems. Advantages: stable labor costs and output, easy to administer, stable pay, less pressure to produce. Disadvantages: no incentive to increase output; extra effort not rewarded.

confusedWith.note: pay tied to amount of output
pay for knowledge and skills

terms.trap: "Time-based systems give stable output but higher pressure" is FALSE: they give less pressure to produce.

terms.short: A pay system that compensates employees according to the amount of output they produce, tying pay directly to performance.
terms.more: Advantages: lower cost per unit, greater output, pay related to effort. Disadvantages: harder wage computation, output must be measured, quality may suffer, pay fluctuates, more scheduling problems.

confusedWith.note: pay for time worked; stable pay
pay for knowledge and skills

terms.trap: "Output-based systems give stable pay" is FALSE: pay fluctuates; stable pay is a time-based advantage.

terms.short: An individual incentive plan in which pay is a direct linear function of output.
terms.more: Once popular, it is now somewhat impractical because of minimum wage legislation. Most current plans add a base rate as a guaranteed floor, with a bonus for output above standard.

confusedWith.note: share productivity gains with employees; team performance

terms.short: Incentive plans that stress sharing productivity gains with employees, emphasizing team rather than individual performance.
terms.more: Some focus only on output; others also reward reductions in material and other costs.

confusedWith.note: individual pay as a linear function of output

terms.short: A pay system in which a portion of workers' pay is based on the knowledge and skills they possess.
terms.more: Three dimensions: horizontal skills (variety of tasks the worker can perform), vertical skills (managerial tasks the worker can perform), and depth skills (quality and productivity results). As companies shift to lean, workers who can do a variety of tasks become valuable.

confusedWith.note: pay for time worked
pay for amount of output

terms.trap: "Horizontal skills are the managerial tasks a worker can perform" is FALSE: horizontal is task variety; vertical is managerial tasks.

terms.short: Analyzing how a job gets done, moving from the overall operation to specific details of workplace arrangement and movements.
terms.more: Seven steps: identify the operation; discuss with operator and supervisor; study and document the present method; analyze the job; propose new methods; implement; follow up. It is done for both existing and new jobs.

confusedWith.note: job content: what, who, how, where
how long a job should take

terms.short: Chart used to examine the overall sequence of an operation by focusing on movements of the operator or flow of materials.
terms.more: Helps identify nonproductive parts of the process: delays, temporary storages, and distances traveled.

confusedWith.note: busy and idle times of operator and machine
simultaneous motions of the hands

terms.trap: "A flow process chart shows when the operator and machine are busy or idle" is FALSE: that's the worker-machine chart.

terms.short: Chart showing the portions of a work cycle during which an operator and equipment are busy or idle.
terms.more: One use is determining how many machines an operator can manage. It highlights worker and machine utilization.

confusedWith.note: overall sequence; operator or material movement
simultaneous motions of the hands

terms.trap: "A worker-machine chart examines the overall sequence of an operation" is FALSE: that's the flow process chart.

terms.short: Systematic study of the human motions used to perform an operation, to eliminate unnecessary motions and find the best sequence.
terms.more: Evolved from Frank Gilbreth's bricklaying work. The four most-used techniques: motion study principles, analysis of therbligs, micromotion study, and charts.

confusedWith.note: how a job is done, from the overall operation down
how long a job should take

terms.short: Guidelines, from Gilbreth's work, for designing motion-efficient work procedures.
terms.more: Three categories: use of the human body; arrangement and conditions of the workplace; design of tools and equipment. Example: continuous curved motions are preferable to straight-line motions with sudden sharp changes.

confusedWith.note: basic elemental motions
motion pictures and slow motion

terms.trap: "Straight-line motions with sharp changes are preferable" is FALSE: continuous curved motions are preferable, and hands should not be idle at the same time.

terms.short: Basic elemental motions that make up a job; the name is Gilbreth spelled backward (except th).
terms.more: Examples: search, select, grasp, hold, transport load, release load, inspect, position, plan, rest, delay. Describing a job in therbligs is justified for short, repetitive jobs.

confusedWith.note: guidelines for motion-efficient procedures
motion pictures and slow motion

terms.short: Use of motion pictures and slow motion to study motions otherwise too rapid to analyze; introduced by Frank and Lillian Gilbreth.
terms.more: Films give a permanent record for training and settling job disputes. Cost limits its use to repetitive activities or where justified, such as surgery.

confusedWith.note: guidelines for motion-efficient procedures
basic elemental motions

terms.short: Simultaneous motion chart: a chart that studies the simultaneous motions of the hands.
terms.more: Invaluable for data entry, sewing, surgical and dental procedures, and certain assembly.

confusedWith.note: overall sequence; operator or material movement
busy and idle times of operator and machine

terms.short: Determining how long it should take to complete a job.
terms.more: The four most commonly used methods: stopwatch time study, historical times, predetermined data, and work sampling. Job times feed capacity planning, workforce planning, labor cost estimates, scheduling, budgeting, and incentive design.

confusedWith.note: job content
how a job is performed

terms.trap: "Methods analysis determines how long a job should take" is FALSE: that's work measurement.

terms.short: Time it should take a qualified worker, at a sustainable rate, to complete a task using given methods, tools, materials, and workplace arrangement.
terms.more: Computed as normal time times an allowance factor. Changes in product design or methods should trigger a new time study.

confusedWith.note: average of recorded times
observed time times performance rating

terms.short: Developing a time standard from observations of one worker over a number of cycles, then applying it to all others doing the task.
terms.more: Introduced by Frederick Winslow Taylor; especially appropriate for short, repetitive tasks. Four steps: define the task and inform the worker; determine the number of cycles; time the job and rate performance; compute standard time.

confusedWith.note: random brief observations; best for nonrepetitive jobs
firm's own historical data
published data such as MTM

terms.trap: "Stopwatch time study is best for nonrepetitive jobs" is FALSE: it suits short, repetitive tasks; work sampling suits nonrepetitive jobs.

terms.short: In a time study, the average of the recorded times.

confusedWith.note: observed time adjusted for worker performance
normal time times allowance factor

terms.short: Observed time adjusted for worker performance by multiplying it by the performance rating.
terms.more: A normal rating is 1.00. Performance rating is subjective and a source of considerable labor-management conflict.

confusedWith.note: average of recorded times
normal time times allowance factor

terms.short: In the typical allowance percentages (Table 7.4), the two constant allowances: personal (5%) and basic fatigue (4%).

confusedWith.note: depend on job conditions such as standing, force, light, noise

terms.trap: "Personal and fatigue allowances are variable allowances" is FALSE: they are constant allowances.

terms.short: Allowances that depend on job conditions, such as standing, abnormal position, use of force, bad light, noise, or monotony.
terms.more: The full list: standing, abnormal position, use of force, bad light, atmospheric conditions, close attention, noise level, mental strain, monotony, tediousness.

confusedWith.note: personal 5% and basic fatigue 4%

terms.short: Time standards derived from a firm's own historical time study data on elements common to many jobs.
terms.more: Advantages: savings in cost and effort, less disruption of work, and no performance ratings needed. Disadvantages: times may not exist for enough elements, and file times may be biased or inaccurate.

confusedWith.note: published data such as MTM

terms.trap: "Standard elemental times come from published data like MTM" is FALSE: they come from the firm's own historical data; MTM is predetermined.

terms.short: Published data, based on extensive research, that give standard elemental times; methods-time measurement (MTM) is a common system.
terms.more: Advantages: based on many workers under controlled conditions, no performance rating, no disruption, and standards can be set before a job is done.

confusedWith.note: the firm's own historical data
observes one worker; requires rating

terms.trap: "Predetermined standards require rating worker performance" is FALSE: no rating is needed, and standards can be set before the job is done.

terms.short: A common predetermined time standards system developed by the Methods Engineering Council, with tables of times for basic elemental motions.
terms.more: The analyst divides a job into elements (reach, move, turn, disengage), measures distances, rates the difficulty, looks up times, and sums them.

terms.short: Technique for estimating the proportion of time a worker or machine spends on various activities and in idle time.
terms.more: Uses brief observations at random intervals, with no timing or continuous observation. Two primary uses: ratio-delay studies and analysis of nonrepetitive jobs.

confusedWith.note: times one worker over cycles; short, repetitive tasks

terms.trap: "Work sampling is best for short, repetitive tasks" is FALSE: that's stopwatch time study; work sampling suits nonrepetitive jobs and needs no timing device.

terms.short: A primary use of work sampling: finding the percentage of a worker's time with unavoidable delays, or the proportion of time a machine is idle.
terms.more: Example: the proportion of time hospital X-ray equipment is not in use.

terms.short: A table of unordered numbers used to set random observation times for work sampling.
terms.more: Digits give the day, hour, and minute of each observation; the starting point should vary between studies so workers can't learn the times.

terms.short: Profit-oriented organizations base location decisions on profit potential; nonprofits strive for a balance between cost and level of customer service.
terms.more: Most organizations do not set out to find the one best location; they hope to find a number of acceptable locations from which to choose, since there are often too many possibilities for an exhaustive search.
terms.trap: "Organizations always seek the single optimal location" is FALSE: they usually look for several acceptable locations. Swapping the profit and nonprofit objectives is also false.

terms.short: The four choices an existing company has when considering location: expand, add a location, move, or do nothing.
terms.more: The 4 options: expand an existing facility; add new locations while retaining existing ones; shut down at one location and move to another; do nothing (maintain the status quo). Expansion costs are often less than the other alternatives.
terms.trap: "Do nothing is not a legitimate location option" is FALSE: it is one of the four options. "Expansion is usually the most expensive option" is also FALSE: expansion costs are often less.

terms.short: When a new location simply draws business from one of the organization's own existing locations.
terms.more: Example: a new mall store that just draws from an existing store. Adding locations requires considering the impact on the total system.

terms.short: Determining the number and location of suppliers, production facilities, warehouses, and distribution centers; a long-term commitment.
terms.more: Location criteria depend on position in the supply chain: the retail end stresses accessibility, demographics, traffic patterns and local customs; the beginning locates near raw materials; the middle locates near suppliers or markets, with storage and distribution favoring a central location.

terms.short: Distributing from a central facility, which gives scale economies and tighter control but sometimes higher transportation costs.

confusedWith.note: more responsive to local needs

terms.trap: Swapping the traits of centralized and decentralized distribution is FALSE: centralized gives scale economies and control; decentralized gives responsiveness to local needs.

terms.short: Distributing from several dispersed facilities, which is more responsive to local needs.

confusedWith.note: scale economies and tighter control, but sometimes higher transportation costs

terms.trap: Swapping the traits of centralized and decentralized distribution is FALSE: decentralized gives responsiveness to local needs; centralized gives scale economies and control.

terms.short: The two key factors that have made global locations easier: trade agreements and technology.
terms.more: Trade agreements reduce barriers such as tariffs and quotas (European Union, World Trade Organization). Technology means advances in communication and information sharing.

confusedWith.note: reasons to go global: markets, cost savings, legal and regulatory, financial, other
drawbacks such as transportation costs and unskilled labor
cultural, political and economic dangers such as IP theft and nationalization

terms.short: Advantages of locating abroad: markets, cost savings, legal and regulatory, financial, and other; not all apply to every situation.
terms.more: Markets: expand or better serve customers. Cost savings: transportation, labor, raw materials, taxes. Legal and regulatory: more favorable laws. Financial: avoid currency changes and tariffs, government incentives. Other: new ideas and perspectives.

confusedWith.note: trade agreements and technology, which make globalizing easier
drawbacks of locating abroad
cultural, political and economic dangers

terms.short: The book's six drawbacks of locating abroad: transportation costs, security costs, unskilled labor, import restrictions, criticisms, and productivity.
terms.more: Transportation costs and low labor productivity can offset labor or material savings. Criticisms refer to cost savings through unfair practices such as sweatshops and child labor; import restrictions, security costs and unskilled labor (extra training, lower quality) are the others.

confusedWith.note: the separate list of risks: IP, political, terrorism, economic, legal, ethical, cultural, quality, supply chain
advantages of locating abroad

terms.trap: "Transportation costs and unskilled labor are risks of global locations" is FALSE: the book lists them as disadvantages.

terms.short: The most troublesome cultural, political and economic dangers of operating abroad, from intellectual property theft to nationalization.
terms.more: The list: protecting intellectual property rights, political (including nationalization), terrorism, economic, legal, ethical (corruption and bribery), cultural, quality, and supply chain issues.

confusedWith.note: transportation costs, security costs, unskilled labor, import restrictions, criticisms, productivity
trade agreements and technology

terms.trap: "Unskilled labor is a risk of global locations" is FALSE: it is a disadvantage. Nationalization of facilities is a political risk.

terms.term: General procedure for making location decisions
terms.section: 8.4 General Procedure for Making Location Decisions
terms.short: Decide on criteria, identify important factors, develop alternatives narrowing from country to region to community to site, then evaluate and select.
terms.more: Deciding on the criteria is simply a matter of managerial preference. New or small organizations tend to be informal; large, established companies are more formal and consider a wider range of locations.
terms.trap: Reversing the narrowing order is FALSE: it runs country, then region, then community, then site.

terms.section: 8.5 Identifying a Country, Region, Community, and Site
terms.short: The few factors that often dominate manufacturing location choices: abundant energy and water, proximity to raw materials, and transportation costs.
terms.more: Example: nuclear reactors need water for cooling and inexpensive land; steel and aluminum need large amounts of electricity.

confusedWith.note: market related: traffic patterns, convenience, competitors' locations, proximity to market

terms.trap: Swapping manufacturing and service dominating factors is FALSE: manufacturing is driven by energy, water, raw materials and transportation; service by market-related factors.

terms.section: 8.5 Identifying a Country, Region, Community, and Site
terms.short: The market-related factors that often dominate service location choices: traffic patterns, convenience, competitors' locations, and proximity to market.
terms.more: Example: Hertz and Avis locate near airports and midcity.

confusedWith.note: energy, water, proximity to raw materials, transportation costs

terms.trap: Swapping manufacturing and service dominating factors is FALSE: service is driven by market-related factors.

terms.section: 8.5 Identifying a Country, Region, Community, and Site
terms.short: The adjustment difficulty transferred employees face when moving to a very different place, a human factor in location decisions.
terms.more: Examples: moving between a big city and a rural area, or to a different climate.

terms.section: 8.5 Identifying a Country, Region, Community, and Site
terms.short: Government requirements that a portion of a product be produced or sourced locally; a government factor in choosing a foreign location.
terms.more: Listed in Table 8.1 under Government, alongside policies on foreign ownership, import and currency restrictions, environmental regulations, local product standards, liability laws and stability issues.

terms.section: 8.5 Identifying a Country, Region, Community, and Site
terms.short: Setting a transfer price that keeps most profit in a foreign subsidiary, avoiding or delaying taxes until returned as dividends.
terms.more: One reason U.S. firms set up foreign subsidiaries, along with low labor rates and low tariffs shipping into the U.S.

terms.section: 8.5 Identifying a Country, Region, Community, and Site
terms.short: The risk that fluctuating exchange rates change supply costs and converted profits when a firm must transact in a local currency.

terms.term: Reasons to locate near raw materials
terms.section: 8.5 Identifying a Country, Region, Community, and Site
terms.short: Three primary reasons to locate near or at the source of raw materials: necessity, perishability, and transportation costs.
terms.more: Necessity: mining, farming, forestry, fishing. Perishability: canning or freezing fresh produce, dairy processing, baking. Transportation costs: processing eliminates much of the bulk (aluminum reduction, cheese making, paper production).
terms.trap: "Cheese making locates near raw materials because of perishability" is FALSE: cheese, paper and aluminum are bulk-reduction (transportation cost) examples; dairy and baking are perishability.

terms.section: 8.5 Identifying a Country, Region, Community, and Site
terms.short: Location factors at the region level: location of raw materials or supplies, location of markets, and labor.
terms.more: Labor factors include cost and availability, wage rates, productivity and attitudes toward work, and managerial attitudes regarding unions. Climate is also discussed as a factor when identifying a region.

confusedWith.note: quality of life, services, attitudes, taxes, environmental regulations, utilities, development support
land, transportation, zoning

terms.trap: Placing labor, raw materials or markets at the community or site level is FALSE: in Table 8.2 they are regional factors.

terms.section: 8.5 Identifying a Country, Region, Community, and Site
terms.short: Location factors at the community level: quality of life, services, attitudes, taxes, environmental regulations, utilities, and development support.
terms.more: Development support includes bond issues, tax abatements, low-cost loans and grants. Community size matters if the firm would be a major employer.

confusedWith.note: raw materials, markets, labor
land, transportation, zoning

terms.trap: "Taxes, utilities and development support are site factors" is FALSE: in Table 8.2, taxes, utilities, quality of life and development support are community factors.

terms.section: 8.5 Identifying a Country, Region, Community, and Site
terms.short: The primary site considerations: land, transportation, and zoning or other restrictions.
terms.more: Because of the long-term commitment, land cost may be secondary to room for expansion, utility and sewer capacities, and sufficient parking. Access roads and rail spurs matter.

confusedWith.note: raw materials, markets, labor
quality of life, services, attitudes, taxes, utilities, development support

terms.trap: Placing zoning at the community or regional level is FALSE: zoning is a site factor.

terms.section: 8.5 Identifying a Country, Region, Community, and Site
terms.short: A developed area suited to light manufacturing or assembly, warehouses, and customer service facilities.
terms.more: Pros: land already developed (power, water, sewer) and zoning needs no special attention. Cons: may restrict kinds of activities, stringent building regulations, and may lack adequate allowance for expansion.

terms.section: 8.5 Identifying a Country, Region, Community, and Site
terms.short: A small factory with a narrow product focus located near major markets to reduce response time.
terms.more: Reflects a trend in light manufacturing (electronics), where low-cost labor is becoming less important than nearness to markets.

terms.section: 8.5 Identifying a Country, Region, Community, and Site
terms.short: Entire products or product lines are produced in separate plants, each usually supplying the entire domestic market.
terms.more: Essentially decentralized; specialization yields economies of scale and lower operating costs than multipurpose plants.

confusedWith.note: plants serve a geographic segment with most or all products
plants handle different aspects of a process
flexible plants handling a range of products

terms.section: 8.5 Identifying a Country, Region, Community, and Site
terms.short: Plants serve a particular geographic segment of the market, each producing most or all of the company's products for that area.
terms.more: Higher operating costs than product plants, but significant shipping savings; desirable when shipping costs are high. Gives rapid delivery and response to local needs; requires centralized coordination.

confusedWith.note: each plant makes a product line for the entire domestic market
plants handle different aspects of a process
flexible plants handling a range of products

terms.trap: "Market area plants have lower operating costs than product plants" is FALSE: their operating costs tend to be higher, offset by shipping savings.

terms.section: 8.5 Identifying a Country, Region, Community, and Site
terms.short: Plants concentrate on different aspects of a process, such as automakers making engines, transmissions, and body stamping in separate plants.
terms.more: Best for products with numerous components. Coordination is a major issue requiring highly informed, centralized administration; benefits from economies of scale but adds shipping costs.

confusedWith.note: each plant makes entire products or product lines
plants serve a geographic segment
flexible plants handling a range of products

terms.section: 8.5 Identifying a Country, Region, Community, and Site
terms.short: Plants are flexible and capable of handling a range of products, allowing quick response to product or market changes.
terms.more: Can be less productive than a more focused approach.

confusedWith.note: each plant specializes in a product line
plants serve a geographic segment
plants handle different aspects of a process

terms.section: 8.5 Identifying a Country, Region, Community, and Site
terms.short: A computer-based tool for collecting, storing, retrieving, and displaying demographic and other data on maps.
terms.more: Relies on integrated hardware, software, data and trained personnel. Business uses include logistics, publishers, real estate, banks, insurance, retailers, utilities and emergency services.

terms.short: Manufacturing and distribution location decisions tend to focus on costs: transportation, energy, labor, and building or leasing.

confusedWith.note: the service and retail focus on demographics, drawing area, competition, traffic, access

terms.trap: "Service and retail locations tend to be cost focused" is FALSE: manufacturers are cost focused; service and retail are revenue focused.

terms.short: Service and retail location decisions tend to focus on profit or revenue: demographics, drawing area, competition, traffic, and customer access.
terms.more: Demographics include age, income and education; customer access includes parking.

confusedWith.note: the manufacturing and distribution focus

terms.trap: "Manufacturing locations tend to be revenue focused" is FALSE: manufacturing is cost focused; service and retail are revenue focused.

terms.short: When businesses locate near similar businesses, such as auto dealerships near each other or restaurants around malls.
terms.more: Retailers generally prefer locations near other retailers for higher traffic and convenience; a unique business with its own drawing power may not need to consider nearness to competitors. Contrast: in small markets that support only one competitor, firms seek locations without competitors.

terms.short: An economic comparison of locations using fixed and variable costs, plotting total-cost lines to find the lowest cost for expected output.
terms.more: Assumes 4 things: fixed costs constant, variable costs linear, required output closely estimable, and only one product. Lower fixed cost tends to win at low volume; lower variable cost at high volume.

confusedWith.note: minimum shipping cost among multiple sources and destinations
weighted composite score of qualitative and quantitative factors
coordinates weighted by quantities to minimize distribution cost

terms.short: A special-purpose linear programming algorithm that determines the minimum transportation cost that results if a new location is added.
terms.more: Used when shipping from multiple sending points to multiple receiving points; results are combined with cost-volume analysis.

confusedWith.note: compares fixed and variable costs across locations
finds a coordinate location that minimizes distribution cost

terms.short: Evaluating locations by weighting relevant factors, scoring each alternative, and choosing the highest composite score; includes qualitative and quantitative inputs.
terms.more: 6 steps: choose relevant factors; assign weights; decide a common scale and minimum score; score each alternative; multiply weight by score and sum; choose the highest composite unless it fails the minimum.

confusedWith.note: a purely economic comparison of fixed and variable costs
minimizes distribution cost using coordinates

terms.short: A method for locating a facility, such as a distribution center, that minimizes shipping costs or travel time to various destinations.
terms.more: Uses a scale map with coordinates; the origin and scale are unimportant. Equal quantities use simple averages of coordinates; unequal quantities use weighted averages.

confusedWith.note: weighted composite score of many factors
LP algorithm for minimum transportation cost among multiple sources and destinations

terms.trap: "The location of the origin matters" is FALSE: the origin and scale are unimportant. Using simple averages when quantities differ is also false; use weighted averages.

terms.short: The ability of a product or service to consistently meet or exceed customer requirements or expectations.
terms.more: Because customers differ, the working definition is customer-dependent. Performance minus expectations: zero means expectations were met, negative means not met, positive means exceeded.

terms.short: The proactive approach, from the late 1970s, of preventing mistakes in the first place by designing quality into products rather than finding defects.
terms.more: It replaced the reactive quality assurance emphasis on finding and correcting defective products before they reached the market. It links quality and profits, stresses customer satisfaction, and involves all levels of management and workers.

confusedWith.note: the earlier era: find and correct defects before they reach the market (reactive)

terms.trap: "The strategic approach is reactive and inspection-focused" is FALSE: it is proactive, preventing mistakes from occurring.

terms.short: W. Edwards Deming's list of 14 points (Table 9.1); his core message was that the system, not the employees, causes inefficiency and poor quality.
terms.more: Among them: cease dependence on inspection; end awarding business on price alone and work with a single supplier; drive out fear; eliminate slogans, exhortations and targets; eliminate numerical quotas; eliminate the annual rating or merit system.
terms.trap: "Increase inspection," "award business to the lowest bidder," "use multiple suppliers," "set numerical quotas," "use slogans" or "institute annual merit ratings" as Deming points is FALSE: his points say the opposite.

terms.short: Correctable (assignable) causes of variation in output, which Deming distinguished from random common causes in order to reduce variation.

confusedWith.note: random causes of variation

terms.short: Random causes of variation in output, which Deming distinguished from correctable special causes.

confusedWith.note: correctable (assignable) causes

terms.short: Joseph Juran's definition of quality: quality is fitness-for-use.
terms.more: Customers sometimes judge the first four dimensions of product quality (performance, aesthetics, special features, conformance) by fitness for use.
terms.trap: "Fitness-for-use is Deming's definition of quality" is FALSE: it is Juran's.

terms.short: Juran's three parts of quality management: quality planning, quality control and quality improvement.
terms.more: Planning establishes processes capable of meeting standards; control tells when corrective action is needed; improvement finds better ways. Juran also held that about 80% of quality defects are controllable by management.

terms.short: Philip Crosby's concept that any level of defects is too high; do it right the first time and stress prevention.
terms.more: The phrase gained favor in the 1960s from the Martin Company's "perfect" missile. Crosby's book Quality Is Free argued quality efforts more than pay for themselves by reducing costs.
terms.trap: "Zero defects was developed by Deming or Juran" is FALSE: it is Crosby's concept, as is "quality is free".

terms.short: Genichi Taguchi's view that any deviation from the target value is poor quality, with cost growing the farther output is from target.
terms.more: The traditional view held that output within specifications has no cost. Reducing inherent variation lowers the cost of poor quality and the loss to society.
terms.trap: "Taguchi holds that output within specs has zero cost" is FALSE: that is the traditional view; Taguchi says any deviation from target has a cost.

terms.short: The next person or operation in the process within the organization; Ishikawa was first to call attention to it.
terms.more: TQM includes both the internal customer and the external customer (end user) when finding out what customers want.

terms.short: The nine dimensions used to define the quality of a good (product); they differ somewhat from those for services.
terms.more: The nine: performance, aesthetics, special features, conformance, reliability (dependable performance, infrequent repairs), durability (performance over time, useful life), perceived quality (indirect, e.g. reputation), serviceability, consistency.

confusedWith.note: a different list of nine for services

terms.trap: "Price is a dimension of quality" is FALSE: price is not on the list.

terms.short: The nine dimensions used to define the quality of a service; they differ somewhat from those for goods.
terms.more: The nine: convenience, reliability, responsiveness (willingness to help), time, assurance (knowledge that conveys trust and confidence), courtesy, tangibles (physical appearance), consistency, expectations.

confusedWith.note: the nine for goods
five dimensions, including empathy

terms.trap: "Knowledgeable personnel conveying trust is reliability" is FALSE: that is assurance.

terms.short: An instrument for getting feedback on an organization's ability to provide quality service, built on five dimensions.
terms.more: The five: tangibles, reliability, responsiveness, assurance, empathy. Empathy is not in the nine-dimension list. It looks at gaps, such as between customer expectations and management perceptions of them.

confusedWith.note: the nine-item list, which has no empathy

terms.trap: "Price, convenience or time is a SERVQUAL dimension" is FALSE: the five are tangibles, reliability, responsiveness, assurance, empathy.

terms.short: The four primary things that determine quality: design, conformance to design, ease of use, and service after delivery.
terms.more: The design phase is the starting point for the quality eventually achieved. The best workmanship can't overcome an inadequate design, and a superior design can't offset poor workmanship.

terms.short: The intention of designers to include or exclude certain features in a product or service.
terms.more: Example for a car: size, appearance, roominess, fuel economy, comfort, materials.

confusedWith.note: the degree to which output achieves the designers' intent

terms.trap: "Quality of design is the degree to which goods conform to the designers' intent" is FALSE: that is quality of conformance.

terms.short: The degree to which goods and services conform to (achieve) the intent of the designers.
terms.more: Affected by equipment capability, worker skills and training, how well the design lends itself to production, monitoring and corrective action. The key is reducing variability in process outputs.

confusedWith.note: the designers' intention to include or exclude features

terms.trap: "Quality of conformance is the designers' intention to include or exclude features" is FALSE: that is quality of design.

terms.short: Costs caused by defective parts, products or faulty services; they relate to poor quality.
terms.more: Split into internal failures (found during production, before delivery) and external failures (found after delivery). Appraisal and prevention costs, by contrast, are investments in good quality.

terms.short: Failures from defects discovered during the production process, before delivery to the customer.
terms.more: Costs include lost production time, scrap and rework, investigation costs, equipment damage, employee injury and downtime.

confusedWith.note: discovered after delivery to the customer

terms.trap: "Scrap, rework or downtime are external failure costs" is FALSE: they are internal failure costs.

terms.short: Failures from defects discovered after delivery to the customer.
terms.more: Costs include warranty work, handling complaints, replacements, liability and litigation, returned goods, loss of goodwill and lost sales. They are typically much greater per unit than internal failure costs.

confusedWith.note: discovered during production, before delivery

terms.trap: "Later detection is cheaper" is FALSE: fixing a problem at the customer end costs about five times as much as at design or production.

terms.short: Costs of inspection, testing and other activities to uncover defects or assure there are none.
terms.more: Examples: inspectors, testing, test equipment, labs, quality audits, field testing, interrupting production to take samples.

confusedWith.note: preventing defects, e.g. training, planning, working with vendors

terms.trap: "Training is an appraisal cost" is FALSE: training is a prevention cost.

terms.short: Costs of attempts to prevent defects from occurring, reducing the potential for quality problems.
terms.more: Examples: planning and administration systems, working with vendors, training, quality control procedures, quality improvement programs, data collection and analysis, design costs.

confusedWith.note: inspection, testing, audits to uncover defects

terms.trap: "Working with vendors or training is an appraisal cost" is FALSE: both are prevention costs.

terms.short: An approach focused on the economics of quality efforts, viewing quality improvement projects as investments evaluated with ROI metrics.
Annual U.S. award, administered by NIST, recognizing U.S. role-model organizations for organizationwide excellence.
terms.more: First given in 1988. Seven evaluation areas: leadership; strategy; customers; measurement, analysis, and knowledge management; workforce; operations; results. All applicants get a written summary of strengths and opportunities for improvement.

confusedWith.note: Japan's award, focused on statistical quality control
Europe's top award

terms.trap: "Baldrige is administered by ISO or ASQ, is open to non-U.S. firms, or gives feedback only to winners" is FALSE: it is run by NIST, for U.S. organizations, and all applicants get feedback.

terms.short: Europe's most prestigious award for organizational excellence, at the top of regional and national quality awards.
terms.more: Applicants have often won regional or national awards first.

confusedWith.note: the U.S. award
the Japanese award

terms.short: Japan's highly coveted annual quality award, named for W. Edwards Deming, whose judging focuses mainly on statistical quality control.
terms.more: Given to any company that meets its standards, including companies outside Japan, and also to individuals. It is much narrower in scope than the Baldrige Award, which focuses more on customer satisfaction.

confusedWith.note: U.S.; broader, more customer-satisfaction focus

terms.trap: "Baldrige focuses mainly on statistical quality control" is FALSE: that is the Deming Prize, which is the narrower of the two.

terms.short: International standards for quality management: what an organization does to ensure its products or services conform to customers' requirements.
terms.more: Relates to processes, not products. Registered companies face ongoing audits and must re-register every three years. Its latest version has eight quality management principles.

confusedWith.note: environmental management
office equipment with reused components

terms.trap: "ISO certification is permanent" or "re-registered annually" is FALSE: re-registration is every three years.

terms.short: International standards covering what an organization does to minimize harmful effects to the environment caused by its operations.
terms.more: Three major areas: management systems, operations, and environmental systems. Like ISO 9000, it relates to processes rather than products and stresses continuous improvement.

confusedWith.note: quality management
office equipment with reused components

terms.short: Standard on the quality and performance of office equipment containing reused components, supporting a declaration that it performs equivalent to new.
terms.more: It also covers meeting safety and environmental criteria.

confusedWith.note: quality management
environmental management

terms.short: A quest for quality in an organization, built on continuous improvement, involvement of everyone, and the goal of customer satisfaction.
terms.more: TQM is intended to prevent poor quality and is about the culture of an organization, not merely a collection of techniques. Compared with a traditional culture it is process oriented, balances long and short term, and treats suppliers as partners.
terms.trap: "TQM is product oriented" or "emphasizes short-term objectives" is FALSE: TQM is process oriented and balances long and short term.

terms.short: Incorporating elements into product or service design that make it virtually impossible for an employee or customer to do something incorrectly.
terms.more: The Japanese term is poka-yoke; also called mistake-proofing. Examples: parts that fit together only one way; appliance plugs that insert only the correct way.

terms.short: A philosophy that seeks to improve all factors of converting inputs into outputs on an ongoing basis, never-ending.
terms.more: "Just because it isn't broke doesn't mean it can't be improved." It covers equipment, methods, materials and people. The Japanese term is kaizen.

confusedWith.note: comparing to the best, in any industry

terms.trap: "Continuous improvement originated in Japan" is FALSE: it originated in the U.S. but became a cornerstone of the Japanese approach.

terms.section: 14.1 Introduction to Lean Operations and JIT
terms.short: Continuous improvement of the system: there is always room for improvement, so the effort is ongoing.
terms.more: Its ten tenets include: improvement is gradual and continuous, everyone is involved, it is built on a cheap strategy, it is supported by a visual system, and it is process oriented.

confusedWith.note: waste
workload leveling

terms.trap: "Kaizen relies on large, infrequent breakthroughs" is FALSE: it is gradual and continuous, cheap, involves everyone, and is process (not results) oriented.

terms.short: Identifying organizations that are best at something and studying how they do it, as an element of TQM.
terms.more: The organization need not be in the same line of business: Xerox benchmarked L.L. Bean for order filling.
terms.trap: "The benchmark must be a direct competitor" is FALSE: it need not be in the same line of business.

terms.short: Giving workers responsibility for improvements and the authority to make changes, so decisions are made by those closest to the job.
The philosophy of making each worker responsible for the quality of their own work; all workers become quality inspectors.
terms.more: It places direct responsibility on those who affect quality, removes the adversarial relationship between QC inspectors and production workers, and motivates workers with control and pride.

confusedWith.note: inspection by a QC department

terms.short: Plan-do-study-act: the conceptual basis for problem-solving activities, drawn as a circle; also called the Shewhart cycle or Deming wheel.
terms.more: Plan the improvement; do it on a small scale if possible; study the data against the goals; act by standardizing the method if successful, or revising and repeating, or ceasing, if not.
terms.trap: "Do means implement company-wide immediately" or "PDSA is Juran's" is FALSE: do is small scale if possible, and it is the Shewhart cycle or Deming wheel.

terms.short: A systematic approach to improving a process, involving documentation, measurement and analysis.
terms.more: Three phases: map the process (including a flowchart), analyze the process, redesign the process. Typical goals include higher customer satisfaction and quality, and less waste, cost and processing time.

terms.short: Define-measure-analyze-improve-control: the formalized five-step Six Sigma problem-solving process.
terms.more: Define sets objectives; measure finds baseline performance and capability; analyze finds cause-and-effect relationships; improve develops a validated improvement; control sustains it.
terms.trap: "Measure comes before define" or "control means developing modifications" is FALSE: define is first, and developing modifications is the improve step.

terms.short: Six Sigma project team leaders responsible for implementing process improvement projects; they play the pivotal role.
terms.more: Typically four weeks of training, an exam and completed projects. Champions rank projects and manage resources; master black belts teach and mentor black belts; green belts are project team members.

confusedWith.note: teachers and mentors of black belts
project team members

terms.trap: "Black belts mentor and teach the other black belts" is FALSE: that is master black belts.

terms.short: The first seven of the chapter's eight visualization tools for problem solving and process improvement.
terms.more: The seven: flowcharts, check sheets, histograms, Pareto analysis, scatter diagrams, control charts, cause-and-effect diagrams. Run charts are the eighth tool.
terms.trap: "Run charts, brainstorming or benchmarking are among the seven basic tools" is FALSE: run chart is the eighth tool, and the others are idea-generation methods.

terms.short: A visual representation of a process that helps identify points where problems might occur.
terms.more: Diamonds are decision points, rectangles are procedures, and arrows show the direction of flow.

terms.short: A simple tool for problem identification: a format for recording and organizing data, often with checkmarks.
terms.more: Common forms tally the type of defect (sometimes by time of day) or the location of defects.

terms.short: A chart of an empirical frequency distribution, showing the symmetry, range and unusual values of observed data.
terms.more: Two peaks suggest two distributions with different centers, such as two workers or two suppliers with different quality.

terms.short: A technique for classifying problem areas by importance and focusing attention on the most important ones.
terms.more: Based on the 80-20 rule: relatively few factors account for a large share of cases. A Pareto chart arranges categories in order of frequency; it is also used for before-and-after comparisons.

terms.short: A graph showing the degree and direction of the relationship (correlation) between two variables.
terms.more: Correlation can be positive (upward-sloping) or negative (downward-sloping). Higher correlation means less scatter.

terms.short: A time-ordered plot of sample statistics, developed by Walter Shewhart, used to determine whether there are nonrandom variations in sample statistics.
terms.more: It has upper and lower control limits. Four commonly used charts: two for variables (mean, range) and two for attributes (p, c). A point on or outside a limit suggests nonrandomness, so halt the process and find the cause.
terms.trap: "All points within the control limits proves the process is in control" is FALSE: it is necessary but not sufficient, because patterns may still exist.

terms.short: A structured diagram for searching for the possible causes of a problem by organizing them into categories of factors.
terms.more: Also called a fishbone or Ishikawa diagram, after Kaoru Ishikawa. Often used after brainstorming to organize ideas.

terms.short: A tool that tracks the values of a variable over time to reveal trends or other patterns.
terms.more: Its advantages are ease of construction and interpretation.

confusedWith.note: detects random vs correctable variation

terms.trap: "The run chart is one of the seven basic quality tools" is FALSE: the book lists it as the eighth tool.

terms.short: A technique in which a group generates a free flow of ideas in a relaxed atmosphere, without criticism.
terms.more: For success, criticism is absent, no one member dominates, and all ideas are welcome. Structured brainstorming ensures everyone participates.
terms.trap: "Ideas are evaluated or criticized as they are offered" is FALSE: criticism is absent.

terms.short: Groups of workers who meet periodically to discuss ways of improving products and processes.
terms.more: Usually less structured and more informal than continuous improvement teams, and with very little authority to make more than minor changes. Kaoru Ishikawa implemented them.

confusedWith.note: sometimes given a great deal of authority (empowerment)

terms.short: Measuring an organization's performance on a key customer requirement against the best in the industry, or the best in any industry.
terms.more: It sets a standard for judging performance and a model for learning. Five steps: identify a critical process, identify an organization that excels at it, contact and study it, analyze the data, improve your process.

confusedWith.note: incremental, ongoing improvement

terms.short: A process that measures output relative to a standard and takes corrective action when output does not meet standards.
terms.more: Its purpose is to assure that processes are performing in an acceptable manner. Acceptable output means no action; unacceptable output means corrective action. Quality control is concerned with the quality of conformance.
terms.trap: "Random variation can be eliminated with corrective action" is FALSE: random variation is natural and cannot be corrected; only nonrandom variation can.

terms.short: Quality assurance that relies primarily on inspection of lots (batches) of items before or after production.
terms.more: Inspection before and after production is acceptance sampling; inspection during production is process control. It is the least progressive stage in the evolution of quality assurance.

confusedWith.note: quality control efforts that occur during production

terms.trap: "Inspection during production is acceptance sampling" is FALSE: before and after production is acceptance sampling; during production is process control.

terms.short: The evolution from inspecting lots, to corrective action during production, to building quality into the process.
terms.more: Three stages, least to most progressive: inspection of lots before/after production (acceptance sampling), corrective action during production (process control), quality built into the process (continuous improvement). The best companies design quality into the process.

terms.short: An appraisal activity that compares goods or services to a standard, to determine whether output is acceptable.
terms.more: Little is needed for well-designed processes, but it cannot be completely eliminated; outsourcing increased its significance. Four basic issues: how much and how often, at what points, centralized or on-site, and attributes or variables.
terms.trap: "100% inspection guarantees zero defects pass" is FALSE: for manual inspection, even 100% inspection does not guarantee all defects will be found.

terms.short: The four decisions in planning inspection: how much and how often, where, centralized or on-site, and attributes or variables.
terms.more: The four: (1) how much to inspect and how often; (2) at what points in the process; (3) centralized (lab/off-site) or on-site; (4) whether data come from attributes (counted) or variables (measured).
terms.trap: "Operations with high human involvement need less inspection than mechanical operations" is FALSE: they need more, because mechanical operations are more reliable.

terms.short: The five places manufacturers typically inspect, chosen because inspection adds cost and should go where it does the most good.
terms.more: The five: raw materials and purchased parts; finished products; before a costly operation; before an irreversible process (e.g., pottery before firing); before a covering process (painting, plating, assemblies).

terms.short: Inspection done on site, favored for quicker decisions and for avoiding damage or alteration of samples in transport.
terms.more: Some inspection must be on site (ship hull cracks). The central issue is whether the advantages of specialized lab tests are worth the time and interruption to obtain results.

confusedWith.note: lab inspection with specialized equipment and a more favorable test environment, but delays

terms.short: Off-site lab inspection, favored for specialized equipment and a better test environment (less noise and confusion, no vibrations, no dust).
terms.more: Examples best done in a lab: medical tests, food samples, metal hardness, lubricant viscosity. The drawback is the time and interruption to obtain results.

confusedWith.note: quicker decisions; avoids loss of sample integrity in transit

terms.short: Quality control during production that evaluates process output to decide if a process is in control or needs corrective action.
terms.more: SPC focuses on detecting departures from randomness. Its two basic tools are control charts and run tests. Its essence is to assure that process output is random so that future output will be random.

confusedWith.note: inspection of lots before or after production

terms.short: A theoretical distribution describing the random variability of sample statistics, most often the normal distribution.
terms.more: Compared with the process distribution, it has the same mean, less variability, and is normal even if the process distribution is not (unless sample size is very small). Larger samples make it narrower.

confusedWith.note: the distribution of individual values, which is wider than the sampling distribution

terms.short: As sample size increases, the distribution of sample averages approaches a normal distribution, regardless of the population's shape.
terms.more: This often holds even for fairly small samples.

terms.short: The six steps of control: define, measure, compare, evaluate, correct, and monitor results.
terms.more: Only characteristics that can be counted or measured are candidates for control. The main task of quality control is to distinguish random from nonrandom variability; management must establish a definition of out of control.

terms.short: The dividing lines between random and nonrandom deviations from the mean; statistical limits on how much sample statistics vary from randomness alone.
terms.more: There is an upper (UCL) and lower (LCL) limit, typically at plus or minus 2 or 3 standard deviations. Control limits are directly related to process variability but have no direct link to specifications.

confusedWith.note: set by design or customers, for individual units of output

terms.trap: "Specifications are derived from control limits" is FALSE: there is no direct link between specifications and control limits.

terms.short: Concluding a process is out of control (nonrandomness present) when only randomness is present; a false alarm.
terms.more: Its probability is the alpha risk, also called producer's risk. Wider limits (3 sigma) reduce Type I error; narrower limits (2 sigma) increase it.

confusedWith.note: concluding in control when the process is really out of control (consumer's risk)

terms.trap: "Wider control limits increase Type I error" is FALSE: wider limits reduce Type I error and increase Type II risk.

terms.short: Concluding a process is in control when it is really out of control, so nonrandom variation goes undetected.
terms.more: Also called consumer's risk. Wider limits (3 sigma) make nonrandom variation harder to detect and so increase Type II risk.

confusedWith.note: concluding out of control when only randomness is present (producer's risk)

terms.trap: "Type II error is the producer's risk" is FALSE: Type II is the consumer's risk; Type I is the producer's risk.

terms.short: Characteristics that are measured, usually on a continuous scale (time, length, width, weight).
terms.more: Variables data use mean (x-bar) and range (R) charts. Measuring costs more per unit than counting but supplies more information, so a much smaller sample is needed for a mean chart than a p-chart.

confusedWith.note: characteristics that are counted, using p- and c-charts

terms.short: Characteristics that are counted rather than measured, such as number of defective parts or calls per day.
terms.more: Attribute data use p-charts and c-charts.

confusedWith.note: characteristics that are measured, using mean and range charts

terms.short: A variables control chart (x-bar chart) that monitors the central tendency of a process and is sensitive to shifts in the process mean.
terms.more: Based on a normal distribution. Only sample means are compared to its limits; individual measurements outside them are irrelevant.

confusedWith.note: monitors dispersion rather than central tendency

terms.short: A variables control chart (R chart) that monitors process dispersion and is sensitive to changes in dispersion.
terms.more: Its underlying sampling distribution is not normal. Mean and range charts complement each other: each can miss what the other catches.
