confusedWith.note: monitors central tendency rather than dispersion

terms.short: An attributes control chart for the fraction (proportion) of defective items in a sample, used when both good and bad can be counted.
terms.more: Used when data fall into two categories (good/bad, pass/fail) with multiple samples of n observations each. Its theoretical basis is the binomial distribution.

confusedWith.note: number of defects per unit; only occurrences countable; Poisson

terms.trap: "Points below the LCL can be ignored because they indicate good quality" is FALSE: they should still be investigated, as they may reflect overuse of resources or lead to an improvement.

terms.short: An attributes control chart for the number of defects per unit, used when only occurrences can be counted, not nonoccurrences.
terms.more: Examples: scratches on a surface, bacteria in a water sample, crimes in a month. Its underlying distribution is the Poisson. A negative computed LCL is set to zero.

confusedWith.note: fraction defective; good and bad both countable; binomial

terms.short: A sequence of observations with a certain characteristic, followed by one or more observations with a different characteristic.
terms.more: For example, A A A B is two runs.

terms.short: A test for patterns in a sequence of observations, supplementing control charts to detect nonrandomness even when all points are within limits.
terms.more: Two widely used run tests: runs up and down, and runs above and below the median. Apply both, since they detect different patterns; if either indicates nonrandomness, it is probably present.
terms.trap: "Only too few runs indicates nonrandomness" is FALSE: too few or too many runs can indicate nonrandomness.

terms.term: Runs above and below the median
terms.short: A run test that labels each observation as above (A) or below (B) the median and compares the number of runs to that expected.

confusedWith.note: labels each observation up or down from the previous one

terms.short: A run test that labels each observation up (U) or down (D) versus the previous one and compares the number of runs to that expected.
terms.more: The first value gets no U or D.

confusedWith.note: labels each observation above or below the median

terms.short: Limits (tolerances) set by engineering design or customer requirements, within which individual units of output must fall to be acceptable.
terms.more: Specifications are stated in terms of output, not the process, so a process can be in statistical control yet not conform to specifications.

confusedWith.note: statistical limits for sample statistics, based on process variability

terms.trap: "A process in control meets specifications" is FALSE: there is no direct link between specifications and control limits, so a process can be in statistical control yet not conform to specifications.

terms.short: The natural or inherent (random) variability in a process, measured by the process standard deviation.
terms.more: Control limits and process variability are directly related; neither has a direct link to specifications.

terms.short: The inherent variability of process output relative to the variation allowed by the design specifications.
terms.more: It is assessed once the process is stable (in control). A process can be in control and still generate unacceptable output if the specs are tighter than it is capable of.
terms.trap: "A stable process is necessarily capable" is FALSE: stability (control) and capability are separate questions.

terms.short: Analysis of a process that is in control to determine whether its range of variation is within design specifications.
terms.more: If it is, the process is called capable. Options when a process is not capable include redesigning it, using an alternative process, 100% inspection, examining the specifications, or outsourcing.

terms.short: The ratio of specification width to process width (6 standard deviations), used for centered processes.
terms.more: The widely accepted standard for capable is Cp of at least 1.33, which gives a cushion. Cp does not involve the process mean, so it is misleading unless the process is centered.

confusedWith.note: takes the process mean into account; used for uncentered processes

terms.trap: "Cp of at least 1.0 is the accepted standard" is FALSE: the widely accepted standard is 1.33.

terms.short: A capability index that takes the process mean into account, used when a process is not centered between its specifications.
terms.more: It is the smaller of (USL minus mean) and (mean minus LSL), each divided by 3 sigma, with the same 1.33 standard. A process may be uncentered if only a range is specified, or nonconformance costs more at one limit.

confusedWith.note: Cp ignores the mean and suits centered processes

terms.trap: "Cp accounts for centering" is FALSE: Cp ignores the mean; Cpk takes it into account.

terms.short: Reducing a process's inherent variability, by five methods: simplify, standardize, make mistake-proof, upgrade equipment, and automate.
terms.more: Benefits include less need for inspection, lower warranty costs, fewer service complaints, higher productivity, and narrower control limits.

terms.short: Three risks in using capability indexes: the process may not be stable, output may not be normal, or Cp is used on an uncentered process.
terms.more: If the process is not stable, the index is meaningless; if output is not normally distributed, inferences about the fraction unacceptable will be incorrect; if the process is not centered but Cp is used, the result is misleading.

terms.short: Intermediate-range capacity planning, typically 2 to 12 months, that sets output, employment and inventory levels for groups of similar products.
terms.more: Some companies plan up to 18 months. Products are aggregated into categories and treated as though a single product; its goal is a production plan that effectively uses resources to match expected demand.

confusedWith.note: the MPS covers about 6-8 weeks and shows specific end items, not product groups
essentially a synonym; S&OP emphasizes integrating financial and operations planning

terms.trap: "Aggregating generally provides a less accurate forecast than forecasting individual items" is FALSE: aggregating generally provides a more accurate forecast.

terms.short: An alternative term for aggregate planning: intermediate-range decisions to balance supply and demand, integrating financial and operations planning.
terms.more: Inputs come from sales (demand forecasts), finance (financial constraints) and operations (capacity constraints). The plan should be shared with supply chain partners.

confusedWith.note: essentially synonyms

terms.trap: "Finance supplies the demand forecasts for S&OP" is FALSE: sales gives demand forecasts, finance gives financial constraints, operations gives capacity constraints.

terms.short: The plan encompassing long-term and intermediate-term planning, setting guidelines from strategies, policies, overall demand forecasts and economic, competitive and political conditions.
terms.more: Its key objective is to coordinate the intermediate plans of marketing, operations and finance (in manufacturing, also engineering and materials management). Planning sequence: business plan, then aggregate plan, then master production schedule.

terms.short: The output of aggregate planning: a general plan setting output, employment and finished-goods inventory levels or service capacities for the intermediate range.
terms.more: It is usually updated periodically, often monthly, giving a rolling planning horizon.

terms.short: Updating the aggregate plan periodically (often monthly) so it always covers the next 12 to 18 months.
terms.more: Similarly, most organizations use rolling 3-, 6-, 9- and 12-month forecasts updated periodically rather than a once-a-year forecast.

terms.short: Aggregate planning strategies that alter demand to match capacity.

confusedWith.note: alter capacity to match demand

terms.trap: "Demand strategies alter capacity to match demand" is FALSE: that's capacity strategies.

terms.short: Aggregate planning strategies that alter capacity to match demand.
terms.more: Mixed strategies alter both demand and capacity.

confusedWith.note: alter demand to match capacity

terms.trap: "Capacity strategies alter demand to match capacity" is FALSE: that's demand strategies.

terms.short: Ways to alter demand to match capacity; they fall mostly in the realm of marketing.
terms.more: The 4 demand options: pricing, promotion, back orders, and new demand.

confusedWith.note: alter capacity; operations realm

terms.trap: "Back orders and pricing are supply options" is FALSE: they are demand options.

terms.short: Ways to alter capacity to match demand; they fall in the realm of operations.
terms.more: The 5 supply options: hire/lay off workers, overtime/slack time, part-time or temporary workers, inventories, and subcontractors. Inventories are more suited to manufacturing than to services.

confusedWith.note: alter demand; marketing realm

terms.trap: "Inventory is a demand option" is FALSE: it is a supply (capacity) option.

terms.short: A demand option that uses price differentials to shift demand from peak to off-peak periods.
terms.more: Examples: weekend hotel rates, night fares, matinees, early-bird specials. The more price elasticity, the more effective pricing is.

confusedWith.note: promotion gives much less control over timing
the service-capacity application of variable pricing to maximize revenue

terms.trap: "The less price elasticity, the more effective pricing is" is FALSE: more elasticity makes pricing more effective.

terms.short: A demand option using advertising, displays and direct marketing; it gives much less control over timing than pricing.
terms.more: Because timing is hard to control, it risks worsening the problem by bringing in demand at the wrong time.

confusedWith.note: pricing gives more control over timing

terms.short: A demand option: taking orders in one period and delivering them in a later period.
terms.more: Success depends on customers' willingness to wait; costs (lost sales, annoyed customers, paperwork) are difficult to pin down. Backlogging is the exception among demand options, being treated with operations' capacity options.

terms.short: A demand option that creates demand to use slack capacity.
terms.more: Examples: fast-food breakfast, landscapers doing snow removal, snowblower makers adding lawn mowers, and insourcing work from another organization.

terms.short: A supply option that acquires temporary capacity from another organization, with less control over output and possibly higher costs and quality problems.
terms.more: The make-or-buy decision depends on capacity, relative expertise, quality considerations, cost, and the amount and stability of demand.

confusedWith.note: supply on a regular, ongoing basis rather than temporary
doing another organization's work during excess capacity

terms.trap: "Subcontracting gives more control over output" is FALSE: it gives less control.

terms.short: An organization doing work for another organization during periods of excess capacity.

confusedWith.note: acquiring temporary capacity from others
another organization supplies you on a regular basis

terms.short: Independent contractors or "gig" workers who are not regular employees, get no benefits, and can be added or subtracted more easily.
terms.more: They give great flexibility.

confusedWith.note: employees with lower wages and benefits, suited to low-to-moderate-skill seasonal work

terms.short: A supply option suited to seasonal work requiring low-to-moderate skills; they cost less in hourly wages and fringe benefits.
terms.more: Unions may regard them unfavorably because they don't pay dues and may lessen union power.

confusedWith.note: not employees, no benefits, easiest to add or subtract

terms.short: A supply option that varies hours worked; less severe and quicker to implement than hiring and layoffs, keeping a steady, skilled workforce.
terms.more: Overtime brings lower productivity, poorer quality, more accidents and higher payroll costs; idle time means less efficient use of machines. Slack time can be used for training, problem solving and process improvement.

confusedWith.note: costly, hurts morale, involves paperwork

terms.trap: "Overtime improves productivity and quality" is FALSE: overtime lowers productivity and quality.

terms.short: A supply option that changes workforce size; its impact depends on how labor intensive operations are.
terms.more: Hiring costs include recruitment, screening and training; layoff costs include severance, unemployment costs and loss of morale among retained workers. An increasing number of organizations view workers as assets rather than variable costs and won't use this approach.

confusedWith.note: less severe, implemented more quickly

terms.section: 11.2 Basic Strategies for Meeting Uneven Demand
terms.short: Keeping capacity constant over the horizon, with inventories, overtime, part-time workers, subcontracting and back orders absorbing demand variations.
terms.more: Works best when inventory carrying costs and backlog costs are relatively low. Advantage: stable output rates and workforce levels; disadvantages: greater inventory costs, more overtime and idle time, varying resource utilization.

confusedWith.note: output matches demand each period

terms.trap: "A level strategy works best when inventory costs are high" is FALSE: level works best when inventory carrying and backlog costs are relatively low.

terms.section: 11.2 Basic Strategies for Meeting Uneven Demand
terms.short: Matching capacity to demand so that planned output for any period equals expected demand for that period.
terms.more: Works best when inventory carrying costs are high and costs of changing capacity are low. Advantages: low inventory investment, high labor utilization; disadvantage: cost of adjusting output rates or workforce levels and lack of stability.

confusedWith.note: capacity kept constant; inventory and back orders absorb variation

terms.trap: "Chase works best when carrying costs are low" is FALSE: chase works best when carrying costs are high and capacity-change costs are low.

terms.section: 11.2 Basic Strategies for Meeting Uneven Demand
terms.short: Strategies with a single focal point: maintaining a level workforce, maintaining a steady output rate, or matching demand period by period (chase).
terms.more: There are 3 pure strategies; the fourth of the four prominent strategies, using a combination of decision variables, is mixed.

confusedWith.note: a combination that lacks a single focus

terms.trap: "Chase is a mixed strategy" is FALSE: chase is one of the three pure strategies.

terms.section: 11.2 Basic Strategies for Meeting Uneven Demand
terms.short: A strategy using a combination of decision variables or of pure strategies, so it lacks a single focal point.
terms.more: It gives greater flexibility and room to experiment, but the absence of clear focus may lead to an erratic approach and employee confusion. In demand and supply options, mixed strategies alter both demand and capacity.

confusedWith.note: single focal point: level workforce, level output, or chase

terms.short: The reactive group of aggregate planning strategies: level production, chase production, and mixed.
terms.more: Level lets inventory absorb variation with back ordering in high-demand periods; chase varies output by hiring/layoffs, overtime or idle time, part-time workers, and subcontracting.

confusedWith.note: proactive: influencing demand

terms.trap: "Supply management is proactive" is FALSE: supply management is reactive; demand management is proactive.

terms.short: The proactive group of aggregate planning strategies: influencing demand through marketing and sales, and producing items with complementary demand patterns.

confusedWith.note: reactive: level, chase, mixed

terms.trap: "Demand management is reactive" is FALSE: demand management is proactive.

terms.short: Customers placing multiple reservations, which inflates demand estimates and can lead to excess capacity.
terms.more: Counting duplicates as true demand overestimates the demand rate; counting their cancellations as lost sales overestimates customers' sensitivity to delay.

terms.short: Informal techniques using simple tables, graphs or spreadsheets to compare projected demand with capacity; the most frequently used, but not necessarily optimal.
terms.more: You can't be sure you have the lowest-cost plan unless every alternative is evaluated; success depends on the planner's resourcefulness and persistence. Spreadsheets are heuristic, intuitively appealing and easy to understand.

confusedWith.note: optimizing
also heuristic, but computerized

terms.trap: "A spreadsheet approach guarantees an optimal plan" is FALSE: it is heuristic and not necessarily optimal.

terms.short: Optimizing methods for allocating scarce resources; in aggregate planning it can be set up as a transportation-type model.
terms.more: Its 3 main limitations: assumed linear relationships, inability to continuously adjust output rates, and the need to specify a single objective.

confusedWith.note: heuristic, not necessarily optimal
heuristic, reasonably acceptable solutions

terms.trap: "Linear programming is a heuristic approach" is FALSE: LP is optimizing.

terms.short: Computerized models tested under a variety of conditions to find reasonably acceptable, not always optimal, solutions.
terms.more: A heuristic (trial-and-error) approach; simulation seems to be gaining favor.

confusedWith.note: optimizing

terms.trap: "Simulation is an optimizing technique" is FALSE: it is heuristic (trial and error).

terms.short: Using variable pricing set relative to capacity availability to maximize revenue: discounts in low demand, higher prices at peaks.
terms.more: Uber calls it surge pricing. Users include airlines, restaurants, theaters, hotels, resorts, cruise lines and parking lots.

confusedWith.note: the demand option of shifting demand off-peak; yield management is its service-capacity application

terms.trap: "Yield management minimizes cost" is FALSE: it maximizes revenue.

terms.short: Breaking down the aggregate plan into specific product requirements to determine labor, materials and inventory requirements.
terms.more: Its result is the master production schedule. Aggregate and disaggregated totals are not always equal in reality, so it may take considerable effort.

terms.short: The result of disaggregation: shows the quantity and timing of specific end items for a horizon of about six to eight weeks.
terms.more: It drives the material requirements planning (MRP) system, and the master schedule is called the heart of production planning and control. In the master scheduling process, the MPS (production requirements) is one of the outputs.

confusedWith.note: intermediate range (2-12 months, up to 18) for product groups

terms.trap: "The MPS covers 12-18 months" is FALSE: that's the aggregate plan; the MPS covers about 6-8 weeks.

terms.short: The central person who evaluates the impact of new orders, provides delivery dates, and deals with production problems.
terms.more: Production problems include evaluating delays or late deliveries, revising the master schedule, and bringing insufficient capacity to the attention of production and marketing. Holds authority in the slushy phase.

terms.short: Testing the feasibility of a proposed master schedule relative to capacities, so no obvious capacity constraints exist.
terms.more: It checks the capacities of production and warehouse facilities, labor and vendors for gross deficiencies.

confusedWith.note: sets capacity levels
driven by the MPS (Ch 12)

terms.short: Divisions of the master schedule horizon into three phases, frozen, slushy and liquid, by how firm the schedule is.
terms.more: They facilitate order promising and order entry. Early periods generally don't allow changes; later periods are more flexible.
terms.trap: "Changes far in the future are the most disruptive" is FALSE: the further out a change, the less tendency to cause problems.

terms.short: The near-term time-fence phase where new orders are nearly impossible; the VP of manufacturing has authority and confidence in promise dates is high.

confusedWith.note: middle; master scheduler; trade-offs
far out; changes easy; tentative dates

terms.trap: "The master scheduler has authority in the frozen phase" is FALSE: the VP of manufacturing does.

terms.short: The time-fence phase a few periods beyond frozen, where order entry requires trade-offs and the master scheduler has authority.
terms.more: Confidence in promise dates is relative, and capacity planning becomes very specific.

confusedWith.note: near term; VP of manufacturing
farthest out; changes easy

terms.short: The farthest-out time-fence phase, where new orders or cancellations are entered with ease and promise dates are tentative.

confusedWith.note: near term; very difficult to change
middle; trade-offs required

terms.trap: "The liquid phase is near-term" is FALSE: it is the farthest out.

terms.short: The three inputs to master scheduling: beginning inventory, forecasts for each period, and customer orders already committed.
terms.more: Requirements for each period are the larger of the forecast and customer orders.
terms.trap: "The bill of materials is one of the three inputs" is FALSE: the inputs are beginning inventory, forecasts and customer orders.

terms.short: The three outputs of master scheduling: projected on-hand inventory, production requirements (the MPS), and uncommitted (available-to-promise) inventory.
terms.trap: "The MPS is an input to master scheduling" is FALSE: it is an output.

terms.short: Inventory projected period by period as the previous week's inventory minus the current week's requirements, the larger of forecast and customer orders.
terms.more: When it becomes negative, a production lot is scheduled.

confusedWith.note: uncommitted inventory marketing can promise

terms.trap: "Requirements are the smaller of forecast and customer orders" is FALSE: they are the larger.

terms.short: Uncommitted inventory that lets marketing make realistic promises to customers about delivery of new orders.
terms.more: It is calculated only for the first week and weeks with an MPS quantity, and updated as new orders are booked.

confusedWith.note: inventory projected after requirements

terms.trap: "ATP is calculated for every week" is FALSE: only for the first week and weeks with an MPS quantity.

terms.short: A stock or store of goods.
terms.more: All businesses carry inventories: goods held for future or potential use. Inventory represents money tied up, typically about 30% of current assets and perhaps as much as 90% of working capital.

terms.short: Demand for items that are ready to be sold or used, such as a finished computer; this chapter's models relate primarily to these.

confusedWith.note: components used to assemble a product, handled by MRP in Ch 13

terms.trap: "The chapter's inventory models are for dependent-demand items" is FALSE: they relate primarily to independent-demand items.

terms.short: Demand for components used to assemble a finished item, such as the parts of a computer; handled by MRP in Chapter 13.

confusedWith.note: finished items ready to be sold or used (this chapter)

terms.trap: "Components are independent-demand items" is FALSE: components used to assemble a product are dependent-demand items.

terms.section: 12.2 The Nature and Importance of Inventories
terms.short: The six kinds of inventory a firm may hold, from raw materials through goods in transit.
terms.more: The 6 types: raw materials and purchased parts; partially completed goods (work-in-process); finished goods (manufacturing) or merchandise (retail); tools and supplies; maintenance and repairs (MRO) inventory; goods-in-transit (pipeline inventory).

terms.section: 12.2 The Nature and Importance of Inventories
terms.short: Partially completed goods; WIP exists because production takes time.

confusedWith.note: goods in transit to warehouses, distributors, or customers

terms.section: 12.2 The Nature and Importance of Inventories
terms.short: Goods in transit to warehouses, distributors, or customers.

confusedWith.note: partially completed goods still in production

terms.trap: "Pipeline inventory is work-in-process" is FALSE: pipeline inventory is goods in transit.

terms.section: 12.2 The Nature and Importance of Inventories
terms.short: The eight reasons firms hold inventory, from meeting anticipated demand to taking advantage of quantity discounts.
terms.more: The 8 functions: meet anticipated customer demand; smooth production requirements; decouple operations; reduce the risk of stockouts; take advantage of order cycles; hedge against price increases; permit operations; take advantage of quantity discounts.

terms.section: 12.2 The Nature and Importance of Inventories
terms.short: Inventory held to satisfy expected, that is average, customer demand.

confusedWith.note: preseason build-up to smooth production
stock in excess of expected demand to cover variability

terms.trap: "Anticipation stock is held for seasonal peaks" is FALSE: anticipation stock covers expected (average) demand; seasonal inventory is the preseason build-up.

terms.section: 12.2 The Nature and Importance of Inventories
terms.short: Inventory built up preseason so a firm can keep output constant while demand follows a seasonal pattern.
terms.more: Examples: greeting cards, winter and summer recreational equipment.

confusedWith.note: held to satisfy expected (average) demand

terms.section: 12.2 The Nature and Importance of Inventories
terms.short: Using inventory buffers between successive operations to keep work continuous despite disruptions such as equipment breakdowns or accidents.
terms.more: Raw-material buffers insulate production from supplier delivery disruptions; finished-goods buffers insulate sales from manufacturing disruptions. Finding and eliminating sources of disruptions can greatly decrease the need for decoupling.
terms.trap: "Decoupling is the same as hedging" is FALSE: decoupling buffers operations against disruptions; hedging buys extra ahead of an anticipated price increase.

terms.section: 12.2 The Nature and Importance of Inventories
terms.short: Average inventory in a system equals the average rate units leave (demand rate) times the average time a unit spends in the system.
terms.more: Example: 5 units per day x 10 days = 50 units.
terms.trap: "Little's Law is a ratio of demand rate to time in the system" is FALSE: it is a product.

terms.section: 12.2 The Nature and Importance of Inventories
terms.short: Annual cost of goods sold divided by average inventory investment: how many times a year inventory is sold.
terms.more: Generally the higher the better, but the higher the profit margins, the lower the acceptable number of turns. High-end retailers (high margins) have low turnover; supermarkets (low margins) have fairly high turnover.

confusedWith.note: days of sales existing inventory can supply; a balance is desirable

terms.trap: "Inventory turnover is average inventory divided by cost of goods sold" is FALSE: it is annual cost of goods sold divided by average inventory investment.

terms.section: 12.2 The Nature and Importance of Inventories
terms.short: The expected number of days of sales that existing inventory can supply.
terms.more: A balance is desirable: a high number means excess inventory; a low number means stockout risk.

confusedWith.note: COGS divided by average inventory; higher is usually better

terms.trap: "More days of inventory on hand is always better" is FALSE: a balance is desirable, since high means excess inventory and low means stockout risk.

terms.short: The five things management needs for effective inventory management, from a tracking system to a classification system for items.
terms.more: The 5 requirements: a system to keep track of inventory on hand and on order; a reliable demand forecast that includes an indication of possible forecast error; knowledge of lead times and lead-time variability; reasonable estimates of holding, ordering, and shortage costs; a classification system for inventory items.
terms.trap: "Effective management requires a demand forecast with no error" is FALSE: it requires a reliable forecast that includes an indication of possible forecast error.

terms.short: A physical count of items at fixed intervals, such as weekly or monthly, to decide how much of each item to order.
terms.more: Advantage: orders for many items occur at the same time, economizing processing and shipping. Disadvantages: lack of control between reviews, and the need to carry extra stock against shortages between reviews.

confusedWith.note: tracks removals continuously and orders a fixed Q at a predetermined minimum

terms.trap: "A periodic system provides tight control between reviews" is FALSE: lack of control between reviews is its disadvantage.

terms.short: A continuous review system that tracks removals continuously; when on hand reaches a predetermined minimum, a fixed quantity Q is ordered.
terms.more: Advantages: control from continuous monitoring, and a fixed order quantity lets management determine an optimal order quantity. Disadvantages: added record-keeping cost, and a physical count must still be performed periodically to verify records.

confusedWith.note: physical count at fixed intervals

terms.trap: "Perpetual systems eliminate the need for physical counts" is FALSE: a physical count must still be performed periodically to verify records.

terms.short: A very elementary perpetual system: withdraw from the first bin until it is empty, then reorder; the second bin covers demand until the order arrives.
terms.more: The second bin also holds an extra cushion (safety stock); its quantity equals the reorder point. Advantage: no need to record each withdrawal. Disadvantage: the reorder card may not be turned in.

confusedWith.note: physical count at fixed intervals, rather than continuous tracking

terms.trap: "The two-bin system is a periodic system" is FALSE: it is an elementary perpetual system.

terms.short: A universal bar code, read by laser scanners, that identifies the manufacturer and the specific item.
terms.more: Scanner benefits to supermarkets: speed and accuracy, continuous information on inventories, reduced need for periodic review and order-size determinations, and improved customer service.

confusedWith.note: alphanumeric code unique to each business

terms.short: A system that electronically records actual sales, giving real-time demand data for forecasting, inventory management, and restocking.
terms.more: POS data are increasingly shared with suppliers for supply chain management.

terms.short: An alphanumeric code unique to each business that identifies item traits such as brand, size, color, price, and customer type.
terms.more: Unlike universal UPCs, SKUs are specific to each business; symbols are arranged from highest priority to lowest relative to what customers want.

confusedWith.note: universal bar code identifying manufacturer and item

terms.trap: "SKUs are universal across retailers" is FALSE: SKUs are unique to each business; UPCs are the universal codes.

terms.short: Tags that transmit data by radio waves to network-connected readers; they carry much more information than bar codes and need no line-of-sight.
terms.more: Walmart, Target, and government agencies require suppliers to use RFID. Widespread adoption, particularly in retail, could take several years (it needs a global standard and cheap disposable tags); main growth continues in nonretail operations.

confusedWith.note: bar codes carry limited information and need direct line-of-sight

terms.trap: "RFID requires line-of-sight" is FALSE: bar codes require direct line-of-sight; RFID does not.

terms.short: The difference between the recorded quantity on hand and the actual quantity on hand.
terms.more: Positive IRI means records show more than actually exists; negative IRI means records show less. Tracking IRI requires periodic physical counts.

terms.short: The amount paid to the vendor or supplier for inventory, which can include shipping; typically the largest of all inventory costs.
terms.trap: "Holding cost is typically the largest inventory cost" is FALSE: purchase cost is typically the largest.

terms.short: Costs of physically having items in storage, such as interest, insurance, obsolescence, pilferage, warehousing, and the opportunity cost of tied-up funds.
terms.more: Only the variable portion is pertinent. Stated as a percentage of unit price or dollars per unit; typical annual holding cost is 20 to 40% or more of item value.

confusedWith.note: fixed per order, including inspecting goods on arrival

terms.trap: "Holding cost is typically the largest inventory cost" is FALSE: purchase cost is typically the largest.

terms.short: Costs of ordering and receiving inventory, such as determining needs, preparing invoices, and inspecting goods on arrival; generally fixed per order.
terms.more: Inspecting incoming goods is an ordering cost, not a holding cost.

confusedWith.note: costs of keeping items in storage
the fixed per-run analog when a firm produces its own inventory

terms.trap: "Ordering cost varies with order size" is FALSE: it is generally a fixed dollar amount per order, regardless of order size.

terms.short: Costs of preparing equipment for a production run, such as adjusting machines or changing cutting tools; a fixed charge per run regardless of run size.
terms.more: Setup costs are analogous to ordering costs when a firm produces its own inventory; they take the place of ordering costs in the EPQ model.

confusedWith.note: fixed per purchase order rather than per production run

terms.short: Costs incurred when demand exceeds supply on hand, such as lost-sale profit, lost goodwill, late charges, backorder costs, or lost production and downtime.
terms.more: Sometimes difficult to measure and may be subjectively estimated. In the single-period model, shortage cost is generally the unrealized profit per unit: revenue per unit minus cost per unit.

confusedWith.note: cost per unit minus salvage value per unit

terms.trap: "Shortage cost equals cost minus salvage value" is FALSE: that is excess cost; shortage cost is generally revenue per unit minus cost per unit.

terms.short: Classifying items by importance, usually annual dollar value (unit value times annual usage), and allocating control effort accordingly.
terms.more: A items: about 10-20% of items but 60-70% of annual dollar value, with frequent reviews and tight control. C items: about 50-60% of items but only 10-15% of value, with loose control (two-bin, bulk orders); B is between. C items are not necessarily unimportant.
terms.trap: "Items are classified by unit price alone" is FALSE: classification uses annual dollar value, unit price times annual usage.

terms.short: A physical count of items in inventory done more often than once a year, to reduce record discrepancies and uncover their causes.
terms.more: Three key questions: How much accuracy is needed? When should cycle counting be performed? Who should do it? ASCM accuracy guidelines are +/-0.2% for A items, +/-1.0% for B, and +/-5.0% for C; A items are counted most frequently.
terms.trap: "C items are counted most often" is FALSE: A items are counted most frequently, B less, and C least.

terms.section: 12.5 How Much to Order: Economic Order Quantity Models
terms.short: The fixed order size that minimizes the sum of annual holding and ordering costs.
terms.more: Total cost is minimized where carrying cost equals ordering cost. The EOQ is fairly robust: the total-cost curve is relatively flat near the EOQ, especially for quantities larger than the EOQ.

confusedWith.note: units received incrementally during production; max inventory below Q

terms.trap: "At the EOQ, carrying cost is twice ordering cost" is FALSE: total cost is minimized where carrying cost equals ordering cost.

terms.term: Assumptions of the basic EOQ model
terms.section: 12.5 How Much to Order: Economic Order Quantity Models
terms.short: Six conditions behind the basic EOQ: one product, known annual demand, evenly spread demand, known constant lead time, single delivery, no quantity discounts.
terms.more: The 6 assumptions (Table 12.1): only one product is involved; annual demand requirements are known; demand is spread evenly throughout the year; lead time is known and constant; each order is received in a single delivery; there are no quantity discounts.
terms.trap: "The basic EOQ model assumes orders are received incrementally" is FALSE: each order is received in a single delivery; incremental receipt is the EPQ model.

terms.section: 12.5 How Much to Order: Economic Order Quantity Models
terms.short: The optimal batch (run) size when a firm produces an item itself and units are received incrementally during production instead of in a single delivery.
terms.more: Used when the production rate exceeds the usage rate. Inventory builds at the production rate minus the usage rate, peaks when production ceases, and never reaches Q. Setup costs replace ordering costs.

confusedWith.note: each order received in a single delivery; max inventory equals Q

terms.trap: "In EPQ, maximum inventory equals the run size Q" is FALSE: usage continually draws off output, so inventory never reaches Q.

terms.section: 12.5 How Much to Order: Economic Order Quantity Models
terms.short: Price reductions for larger orders, offered to induce customers to buy in large quantities.
terms.more: Before taking a discount, ask: Will storage space be available? Will obsolescence or deterioration be an issue? Can we afford to tie up extra funds? If carrying cost is constant there is one common minimum point; if it is a percentage of price, begin with the lowest unit price.
terms.trap: "When carrying cost is a percentage of price, start with the highest price" is FALSE: begin with the lowest unit price.

terms.section: 12.5 How Much to Order: Economic Order Quantity Models
terms.short: The minimum quantity needed to obtain a discounted price.
terms.more: Feasible total cost drops down to a lower-price curve at each price break, giving a stepped total-cost curve.

terms.short: The quantity on hand at which an order is placed: generally expected demand during lead time plus perhaps an extra cushion of safety stock.
terms.more: EOQ answers how much to order; ROP answers when. The 4 determinants: rate of demand, lead time, extent of demand and/or lead-time variability, and degree of stockout risk acceptable to management.

confusedWith.note: orders triggered by time; order size varies

terms.trap: "The ROP works with periodic review" is FALSE: knowing when the ROP is reached requires perpetual monitoring.

terms.short: Inventory intended to meet expected demand.

confusedWith.note: held to reduce stockout probability due to variability

terms.short: Stock held in excess of expected demand to reduce the probability of a stockout due to demand and/or lead-time variability.
terms.more: Depends on average demand and lead time, their variability, and the desired service level. Greater variability or a higher service level means more safety stock; it offsets uncertainty but adds holding cost.

confusedWith.note: inventory intended to meet expected demand

terms.trap: "Safety stock covers expected demand" is FALSE: it is stock in excess of expected demand.

terms.short: Order cycle service level: the probability that demand will not exceed supply during lead time.
terms.more: Service level and stockout risk are complements (service level = 100% minus stockout risk). In the single-period model, service level is the probability demand will not exceed the stocking level, Cs / (Cs + Ce).

confusedWith.note: percentage of demand filled directly from inventory

terms.trap: "A 95% service level means 95% of demand will be satisfied" is FALSE: it means a 95% probability that demand will not exceed supply during lead time.

terms.short: The annual service level: the percentage of demand filled directly from inventory.
terms.more: Example: 990 of 1,000 units filled from stock is a 99% fill rate.

confusedWith.note: order cycle service level: probability of no stockout during lead time

terms.section: 12.7 How Much to Order: Fixed-Order-Interval Model
terms.short: Orders are placed at fixed time intervals, so timing is set and the order size varies with demand.
terms.more: Reasons for use (3): supplier's policy, grouping orders from the same supplier to save shipping, and situations that don't allow continuous monitoring. It must protect over the order interval plus lead time, so it needs more safety stock. Widely used by retailers, especially small ones.

confusedWith.note: quantity trigger; order size fixed, interval varies; protection over lead time only

terms.trap: "The fixed-order-interval model needs less safety stock than the fixed-quantity model" is FALSE: it protects over the order interval plus lead time, so it needs more.

terms.section: 12.7 How Much to Order: Fixed-Order-Interval Model
terms.short: In the fixed-order-interval model, expected demand over the protection interval (order interval plus lead time) plus safety stock.
terms.more: Amount to order = OUL minus amount on hand at reorder time. Because of lead time, actual on-hand inventory will likely never reach the OUL.

terms.short: The "newsboy problem": ordering perishables or items with limited useful life that are not carried over to the next period.
terms.more: Examples: fresh fruit, vegetables, seafood, cut flowers, newspapers, magazines, spare parts for specialized equipment. It balances shortage and excess costs; for discrete stocking levels, stock at the next higher level.
terms.trap: "The single-period model applies to items carried over between periods" is FALSE: it is for items that cannot be carried over.

terms.short: The cost of items left over at the end of the period: original cost per unit minus salvage value per unit.
terms.more: A disposal cost acts as a negative salvage value, which increases excess cost. If excess cost is greater than shortage cost, the service level is below .50 and the optimal stocking level can be less than expected demand.

confusedWith.note: revenue per unit minus cost per unit

terms.trap: "Excess cost equals revenue minus cost" is FALSE: that is shortage cost; excess cost is cost minus salvage value.

terms.short: A flexible system of operation that uses fewer resources (activities, people, inventory, floor space) than a traditional system.
terms.more: Lean systems tend to achieve greater productivity, lower costs, shorter cycle times and higher quality. Lean is both a philosophy and a methodology focused on eliminating waste (non-value-added activities).

confusedWith.note: alternate name emphasizing delivery of goods just as they are needed
emphasizes efficiency of individual operations, leading to unbalanced systems and large inventories

terms.short: Unloading inbound trucks at distributor warehouses directly onto outbound trucks, avoiding warehouse handling and storage costs.
terms.trap: "Cross-docking stores goods in the warehouse" is FALSE: goods move directly onto outbound trucks, avoiding storage.

terms.short: An alternate name for lean systems, owing to highly coordinated activities and delivery of goods just as they are needed.
terms.more: Used mainly in repetitive operations; very little inventory because successive operations are closely coordinated. In its truest sense, a philosophy encompassing every aspect of the process, from design to after the sale.

confusedWith.note: the flexible system using fewer resources; JIT is its alternate name

terms.trap: "JIT is merely a scheduling technique" is FALSE: that is the narrow view; in its truest sense JIT is a philosophy covering every aspect of the process.

terms.term: Three basic elements of lean systems
terms.short: Lean systems are demand-driven, focus on waste reduction, and have a culture dedicated to excellence and continuous improvement.
terms.more: Exactly three elements: demand-driven; focus on waste reduction; culture dedicated to excellence and continuous improvement.

confusedWith.note: the five principles of how lean systems function

terms.trap: "Lean systems are push-driven" is FALSE: they are demand-driven, and there are three elements.

terms.term: Five principles of how lean systems function
terms.section: 14.1 Introduction to Lean Operations and JIT
terms.short: Identify customer values; focus on value-creating processes; eliminate waste to create flow; produce only to customer demand; strive for perfection.
terms.more: Exactly five principles. The value-improvement steps of value stream mapping mirror them.

confusedWith.note: demand-driven; waste reduction focus; culture of excellence and continuous improvement
the three supporting goals of a lean system

terms.trap: "Maximize equipment utilization" or "produce to forecast" as a lean principle is FALSE: the five principles do not include them, and waste is eliminated to create flow, not inventory buffers.

terms.section: 14.1 Introduction to Lean Operations and JIT
terms.short: Toyota's approach that has served as a model for many lean implementations, particularly in manufacturing.
terms.more: Key terms: muda, kanban, heijunka, kaizen and jidoka. Pioneered by Taiichi Ohno and Shigeo Shingo; Toyota studied Ford's River Rouge but built a system that could handle some variety.

terms.section: 14.1 Introduction to Lean Operations and JIT
terms.short: A Toyota-GM joint venture that reopened GM's closed Fremont, California plant and, by 1985, beat every other GM plant on productivity and quality.
terms.more: About 80% of former workers were rehired; white-collar jobs shifted from directing to supporting workers, and small teams were trained to improve performance. Lesson: same workers, different system.

terms.section: 14.1 Introduction to Lean Operations and JIT
terms.short: Waste; minimizing it is perhaps the driving philosophy of lean.

confusedWith.note: continuous improvement
workload leveling

terms.trap: "Muda means continuous improvement" is FALSE: muda is waste; kaizen is continuous improvement, heijunka is leveling, jidoka is quality at the source.

terms.section: 14.1 Introduction to Lean Operations and JIT
terms.short: A manual system that controls the movement of parts and materials by responding to signals of need (demand) for delivery.
terms.more: Kanban is Japanese for "signal" or "visible record." Its major benefit is simplicity; it resembles a two-bin inventory system, and lean can exist without kanban.

confusedWith.note: computerized; handles complex planning; assumes fixed lead times and infinite capacity
controls WIP for the system as a whole rather than individual workstations

terms.trap: "Kanban is computerized" is FALSE: kanban is manual (MRP is computerized), and lean does not require kanban.

terms.section: 14.1 Introduction to Lean Operations and JIT
terms.short: Workload leveling: averaging production volume and variety to achieve a steady flow, because variations in volume lead to waste.

confusedWith.note: continuous improvement
waste

terms.trap: "Heijunka means continuous improvement" is FALSE: heijunka is workload leveling; kaizen is continuous improvement.

terms.section: 14.1 Introduction to Lean Operations and JIT
terms.short: Quality at the source: a machine automatically stops when it detects a bad part, and a worker then stops the line.
terms.more: Also known as autonomation.

confusedWith.note: continuous improvement
signal system for parts movement

terms.trap: "Jidoka is the signal card system for moving parts" is FALSE: that is kanban; jidoka is quality at the source (autonomation).

terms.term: Supporting goals of a lean system
terms.short: Three goals serving lean's ultimate goal of a balanced, smooth, rapid flow: eliminate disruptions, make the system flexible, eliminate waste (especially excess inventory).
terms.more: Disruptions come from poor quality, equipment breakdowns, schedule changes and late deliveries. Long setup and lead times hurt flexibility.

confusedWith.note: the four building blocks that support the goals
the five principles of how lean systems function

terms.trap: "Maximize capacity utilization" or "eliminate all inventory" as a supporting goal is FALSE: there are three goals, and the target is excess inventory.

terms.short: Eight kinds of muda that show where improvement is possible and give targets for continuous improvement.
terms.more: The eight: excess inventory, overproduction, waiting time, unnecessary transporting, processing waste, inefficient work methods, product defects, underused people (mental and creative as well as physical abilities).
terms.trap: "There are seven wastes" is FALSE: this text lists eight, including underused people, which covers mental and creative abilities, not only physical.

terms.short: The four foundations of a lean system: product design, process design, personnel/organizational elements, and manufacturing planning and control.
terms.more: Speed and simplicity are two common threads through all four; data and analytics play a role in each.

confusedWith.note: the three goals the building blocks support

terms.trap: "Supply chain design" or "information technology" as a building block is FALSE: there are exactly four, and neither is one.

terms.short: An extension of standard parts in which modules, clusters of parts treated as a single unit, greatly reduce the number of parts.
terms.more: Simplifies assembly, purchasing, handling and training. One of the four product design elements, with standard parts, quality built in, and concurrent engineering.

terms.short: Automatic detection of defects during production, plus a mechanism for a human to stop production and correct the cause.
terms.more: Also called jidoka; usable with machines or manual operations. Halting forces immediate attention, investigation and corrective action.

confusedWith.note: autonomation is not the same as automation

terms.short: The cycle time needed to match the pace of production to the demand rate; the heartbeat of a lean production system.
terms.more: Takt is German for musical meter. Takt time = net available time / demand; each workstation's work time must be no more than the cycle time, which is set equal to takt time.

confusedWith.note: the time at a workstation, which must be no more than takt time
a different time measure

terms.trap: "Takt time = demand / available time" is FALSE: it is net available time / demand, and takt is German, not Japanese.

terms.short: Water is inventory, rocks are problems and the boat is production: lowering inventory gradually reveals problems, largest first, to be removed.
terms.more: Repeated in the spirit of continuous improvement; as rocks are removed, less water (inventory) is needed.
terms.trap: "The water represents problems" is FALSE: water is inventory; also, the largest rocks appear first and inventory is lowered gradually, not all at once.

terms.short: Mistake proofing: building safeguards into a process to reduce or eliminate the potential for errors (failsafing), credited largely to Shigeo Shingo.
terms.more: Originally called baka-yoke ("foolproofing"), renamed because of its offensive connotation. Examples: parts that attach only in the correct position, fuses and circuit breakers, ATM card-left signals.
terms.trap: "Poka-yoke means foolproofing" is FALSE: that was baka-yoke; poka-yoke means mistake proofing, and it is credited to Shingo, not Deming or Ohno.

terms.short: A Japanese light system signaling problems: green means no problems, amber means a worker is falling a little behind, red means a serious problem.
terms.more: Lets workers and supervisors immediately see when and where problems occur. An andon board shows the real-time status of each car on the line.
terms.trap: Swapping the andon color meanings is FALSE: green = no problems, amber = falling a little behind, red = serious problem.

terms.short: A costing method that identifies traceable costs, assigns them to activities, then charges jobs overhead by their share of activities consumed.
terms.more: Activities include machine setups, inspection, machine hours, direct labor hours and material movement. Not the same as A-B-C inventory classification.

confusedWith.note: traditional method that can give labor-intensive jobs a disproportionate share of overhead

terms.trap: "Lean allocates overhead by direct labor hours" is FALSE: that is the traditional method; lean's alternative is activity-based costing.

terms.short: Scheduling for stable, level daily mix schedules, which may be rate-based rather than quantity-based and stay relatively fixed over a short horizon.
terms.more: Suppliers like level loading because it smooths their demand. The extreme case, one unit of each product in turn, is generally impractical because of excessive setup costs.
terms.trap: "Level loading uses quantity-based schedules that change daily" is FALSE: schedules may be rate-based and are relatively fixed over a short horizon.

terms.short: Scheduling several models in a repeating daily sequence, starting from each model's daily production requirements.
terms.more: Three issues: which sequence (setup time or cost is key), how many cycles per day, and how many units of each model per cycle (limited by lot-size restrictions).

terms.short: The traditional system where finished work is pushed to the next station as it is completed, regardless of that station's readiness.
terms.more: Work may pile up at stations that fall behind. Push systems don't hold arrival rate constant, causing WIP buildups and high cycle-time variability.

confusedWith.note: the following operation controls movement of work

terms.trap: "Push moves work in response to downstream demand" is FALSE: that describes pull; push moves work when completed.

terms.short: A system where control of moving work rests with the following operation, so each station pulls output from the preceding one as needed.
terms.more: Communication moves backward through the system. Pull requires a fairly steady flow of repetitive work; large variations in volume, mix or design undermine it.

confusedWith.note: work moves when completed, regardless of the next station

terms.trap: "In a pull system, communication flows forward" is FALSE: it moves backward, and pull does not work well with highly variable volume or mix.

terms.short: The card that authorizes moving or working on parts; no part or lot can be moved or worked on without one.
terms.more: Two main types: production kanban (produce parts) and conveyance kanban (move parts). If the system is too loose, withdraw kanbans; if too tight, add them.

terms.short: A kanban card that signals the need to produce parts.

confusedWith.note: signals the need to deliver or move parts

terms.trap: Swapping p-kanban and c-kanban is FALSE: production kanban signals produce; conveyance kanban signals move.

terms.short: A kanban card that signals the need to deliver (move) parts to the next work center.

confusedWith.note: signals the need to produce parts

terms.trap: Swapping c-kanban and p-kanban is FALSE: conveyance kanban signals move; production kanban signals produce.

terms.short: A visual management technique using outline shapes to show where tools are stored.
terms.more: One of five other visual techniques: shadow tool boards, scoreboards, work-zone color coding, andon lights, visual maintenance.

terms.short: Controlling WIP for the system as a whole: when a job exits, a new job may enter, keeping WIP constant.
terms.more: Has an advantage with variability, since upstream stations keep working longer after a breakdown, and is easier in mixed-product environments.

confusedWith.note: focuses on individual workstations and specific part numbers; works best in stable environments

terms.trap: "CONWIP controls individual workstations" is FALSE: that is kanban; CONWIP controls the whole system and handles variability better.

terms.short: Lean arrangement of relatively few first-tier suppliers, who work directly with the company or supply major subassemblies and deal with second-tier suppliers.
terms.more: Each tier deals only with those just above or below it, and each bears full responsibility for its portion's quality. Example: one first-tier supplier for a whole electric seat.

confusedWith.note: traditional: hundreds of suppliers as spokes around the company at the hub

terms.trap: "First-tier suppliers supply raw components only" is FALSE: they work directly with the company or supply major subassemblies, and deal with second-tier component suppliers.

terms.short: Miller and Vollmann's idea that non-value-adding transactions in traditional planning and control systems create a tremendous cost burden.
terms.more: Four classes: logistical (ordering, shipping, expediting), balancing (forecasting, planning, scheduling, procurement, order processing), quality, and change (engineering changes, among the most costly transactions).
terms.trap: "Forecasting and scheduling are logistical transactions" is FALSE: they are balancing transactions; expediting and shipping are logistical.

terms.short: Keeping equipment in good condition and replacing parts likely to fail before they fail.
terms.more: Vital in lean because little in-process inventory makes breakdowns extremely disruptive. Workers often maintain their own equipment.

terms.short: Keeping the workplace clean and free of materials not needed for production, which take space and can disrupt flow.
terms.more: Housekeeping is part of the Five Ss.

terms.short: Five behaviors that make the workplace effective: sort, straighten, sweep, standardize, self-discipline.
terms.more: Sort keeps only needed items; straighten organizes for quick access; sweep keeps it clean with regular maintenance; standardize sets standard procedures; self-discipline means understanding the need for an uncluttered workplace.
terms.trap: "Straighten means keeping only needed items" is FALSE: that is sort; this text also uses sweep (not shine) and self-discipline (not sustain).

terms.short: A visual tool that systematically examines the flow of materials and information involved in bringing a product or service to a consumer.
terms.more: Originated at Toyota, where it is called "Material and Information Flow Mapping." Its objective is to increase value to the customer.

confusedWith.note: a questioning approach
going to the actual place

terms.trap: "VSM maps only material flow" is FALSE: it maps materials and information, and it originated at Toyota, not Ford or Motorola.

terms.short: Going to the actual place (gemba) where operations occur, to learn work practices, coach employees and follow up on issues.
terms.more: Guidelines: have a purpose, keep it brief (30-45 minutes), drive out fear. The biggest mistake is wandering on a meet-and-greet basis.

confusedWith.note: maps material and information flow

terms.trap: "Gemba means continuous improvement" is FALSE: gemba means actual place.

terms.short: A process-improvement approach asking five W questions and two H questions to cut cost and waste.
terms.more: The seven: What (subject), Why (purpose), Where (location), When (sequence), Who (people), How (method), How much (cost). Can be used alone or with value stream mapping.

confusedWith.note: a visual map of material and information flow

terms.trap: "5W2H means five H's and two W's" is FALSE: it is five W's and two H's, including How much, and Why relates to purpose, not location.

terms.short: Companies let suppliers manage restocking, with a supplier representative working in the company's plant to ensure appropriate supply.
terms.more: Term popularized by the Bose Corporation; often called vendor-managed inventory (VMI).
terms.trap: "JIT II was popularized by Toyota" is FALSE: it was Bose, and the supplier manages restocking, not the buyer.
